articles.title: Albania: As corruption cases multiply, experts question whether the anti-corruption drive is addressing the causes or just the symptoms
articles.summary: From a former president to the ex-intelligence chief, Albania is prosecuting senior officials at a rate once thought impossible. But do more prosecutions mean less corruption or simply better…

image.caption: Vlora Hyseni, former head of Albania's State Intelligence Service, leaves the offices of Albania's Special Prosecution Office against Corruption and Organized Crime (SPAK), where she answered questions about her alleged involvement in a major corruption scandalImage: Armando Babani/Matrix Images/pic

blocks.text: On September 22, the head of Albania's State Intelligence Service, Vlora Hyseni, was in Baku, Azerbaijan, attending an international conference of intelligence service chiefs. Back in Tirana, the Special Court had ordered her house arrest over two suspected criminal offences: supporting the perpetrator of a crime and disclosure of investigative secrecy.

The investigation into Hyseni emerged from a wider corruption case involving the National Agency for Information Society (AKSHI), the agency responsible for much of Albania's digital public infrastructure.
Prosecutors suspect that she used information available to her as intelligence chief to help a person wanted in that investigation.
Hyseni turned herself in to the Albanian authorities later that day and remains under house arrest as the investigation continues. She has since been dismissed as head of the intelligence service.
Rise in criminal proceedings and investigations
Hyseni's case is the latest in a series of criminal proceedings that have reached unusually high into Albania's political and state establishment.

blocks.caption: Political scientist Afrim Krasniqi says that after the 2016 reform, Albania's new justice institutions were expected to 'focus on high-level corruption and "VIP" cases'Image: Afrim Krasniqi/Privatarchiv

blocks.text: A former president has spent almost two years in detention, a former prime minister is on trial, the mayor of Tirana has been behind bars since early 2025, two former deputy prime ministers under Prime Minister Edi Rama have also faced criminal proceedings, and investigations have been launched into senior officials in agencies controlling large areas of public spending and state infrastructure.
These are all separate cases, but they all involve alleged abuse of public power.
How did Albania get here?
For years, the problem was completely the opposite: High-level corruption in Albania was widely associated with impunity.
This is why bringing senior political figures accused of wrongdoing before the courts became one of the central expectations of the justice reform launched in 2016.

"The expectation was that the new justice institutions would focus on high-level corruption and 'VIP' cases," says Afrim Krasniqi, a political scientist and executive director of the Institute for Political Studies in Tirana. "There were individuals who stood above the law, and impunity was pronounced," he told DW.

blocks.caption: Dorian Matlija says that Albania is 'becoming more effective at punishing corruption after it has occurred, but much less capable of preventing it'Image: Kristi Çavo

blocks.text: The reform fundamentally reshaped Albania's justice system and created new institutions to investigate corruption and organized crime, including the Special Anti-Corruption Structure, SPAK.
But the change was not immediate. Building the new institutions took years, and older cases were often more difficult to investigate.

For Dorian Matlija, a lawyer and executive director of Albanian civil society organization Res Publica, the number of senior officials now facing criminal proceedings does not necessarily mean that corruption is more widespread today than it was in the past.

"What has changed significantly is the institutional reaction," Matlija told DW. "Today, SPAK is a specialized structure with greater independence, stronger capacities and international support, as well as the willingness to undertake investigations that have broken the myth of the untouchability of senior officials."
The other side of accountability
But bringing senior officials before the courts is only one measure of whether institutions are working.

blocks.caption: Albania applied for EU membership in 2009 and was granted candidate status in June 2014. Pictured here: Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama and President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen (both center)Image: Valdrin Xhemaj/REUTERS

blocks.text: By the time a corruption case reaches prosecutors, the alleged abuse has already taken place. For Matlija, this is where Albania's progress is far less clear.
"We are becoming more effective at punishing corruption after it has occurred, but much less capable of preventing it," he said.

Matlija points to the institutions and mechanisms that are supposed to act before a case becomes criminal: administrative controls, audits, conflict-of-interest rules and asset declarations. In his assessment, these have often proved ineffective.

The European Commission's 2025 report on Albania reaches a similar conclusion. It said that SPAK has made "tangible progress towards a solid track record in the fight against corruption." At the same time, the report says that corruption remains widespread and that "the institutional framework for prevention of corruption continued to have a limited impact."
The impact on citizens
The problem is also visible in citizens' encounters with public officials.

In a 2023 survey by the anti-corruption and good governance coalition SELDI (Southeast Europe Leadership for Development and Integrity), 52% of respondents in Albania said they had experienced corruption pressure from public officials, while 40% reported having paid a bribe.

Krasniqi sees the problem in broader political terms. Albania has been governed by Rama's Socialist Party since 2013, and the party currently holds an outright majority in parliament. He argues that this prolonged political dominance has weakened the checks and balances that should constrain the executive.
"We have a deformed system," he said. "The head of the executive controls the executive, parliament and institutions."

He argues that this concentration of power has been accompanied by informal networks of influence, with people outside state institutions able to shape political decisions, legislation and the use of public assets.
Rama has repeatedly maintained that criminal responsibility is individual when investigations have reached senior officials. Responding to the Hyseni case, he returned to the same position.
"When a senior official has opened an account with justice, the case of the former intelligence chief is an individual matter between her and the justice system," Rama said.
What does this mean for Albania's EU accession hopes?

In May, the EU confirmed that the country had met the interim benchmarks for the "fundamentals" cluster, which includes the rule of law, and moved into a phase focused on implementation and lasting results.
Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index shows Albania improving from 33 points in 2012 to 39 in 2025 but still ranking below all EU member states.
For Matlija, Albania's efforts to advance EU integration helped create the conditions that allowed institutions such as SPAK to become stronger and more independent.

"The EU no longer demands only the adoption of laws and reforms, but also concrete and sustainable results. This creates constant pressure for justice institutions to be genuinely effective and independent of political power," he said.

For Krasniqi, this is also where the meaning of European integration lies. Membership, he argues, should not be judged only by Albania's progress through the formal accession process, but by whether the country itself changes.

"The essence should be for Albania, Albanian society and Albanian institutions to change and improve, so that we become worthy of integration," he said. For him, that change should also be felt by citizens through greater social security, prosperity and independence, rather than being just a series of formal achievements.

articles.title: Victoria Bossong claims 800m bronze in Asian Games debut
articles.summary: The fastest in the heats, Victoria Bossong finishes third in the women's 800 final as she delivers the Philippines' second athletics medal in the 2026 Asian Games

blocks.text: REPRESENT. Athletics standout Victoria Bossong in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.
PSC-POC Media Pool
The fastest in the heats, Victoria Bossong finishes third in the women's 800 final as she delivers the Philippines' second athletics medal in the 2026 Asian Games

MANILA, Philippines – Victoria Bossong turned in a slower time in the final but still salvaged an athletics medal for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games as she snagged the bronze in the women’s 800m at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium in Japan on Tuesday, September 29.

The Filipina-American middle-distance specialist clocked 2 minutes and 5.34 seconds to finish third and deliver the Philippines’ second athletics medal in this edition of the quadrennial showpiece after John Cabang Tolentino bagged bronze in the men’s 110m hurdles.
China’s Wu Hongjiao struck gold with 2:04.49, while Bahrain’s Nelly Korir clinched silver with 2:05.16 — the three medalists separated only by less than a second.
Bossong, whose mother, Catalina Atienza, hails from Oriental Mindoro, emerged as the title favorite after posting the fastest time in the heats, where she registered 2:02.34.

A repeat of that time would have netted the 23-year-old Harvard University graduate the Philippines’ first Asian Games gold medal in a track event since the late Lydia de Vega ruled the women’s 100m in the 1986 edition.
But it simply was not meant to be for Bossong, who owns a personal best of 1:58.52 — a time that eclipses the Asian Games record of 1:59.02 set by Kazakhstan’s Margarita Mukasheva in 2014.
Still, Bossong enjoyed a promising debut for the Philippines in a multi-sport event, which came just months after she gained eligibility in July to represent the country. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Israel bans Arab parties from election: What you need to know
articles.summary: Israel's push to ban Arab parties from standing in the upcoming election has been called "another nail in the coffin of democracy." Is there a legal basis for doing this, and what could it mean for…

image.caption: Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party were among those pushing for the banImage: Brendan McDermid/REUTERS

blocks.text: With less than a month until the Israeli elections, a move from the country's Central Elections Committee (CEC) to bar all Arab parties from running has ignited a debate about the relationship between security, national identity and democratic representation in Israel.

Should the bans remain in place when Israel goes to the polls on October 27, Arab citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the country's population, will find themselves without their most likely source of representation in the Israeli parliament, the Knesset.
However, the decision is not final, and the Supreme Court could overrule it in the coming days.
Which Arab parties have been banned from the election?

Perhaps the most high-profile party to be banned is Ra'am, otherwise known as The United Arab List. The party currently holds five of the 120 seats in the Knesset and takes a conservative, Islamic position. Earlier this year it announced that it would allow Jewish candidates to stand for the party, with former Israeli police commissioner and deputy minister of national security, Yoav Segalovitz, set to run if the party is permitted.
The ban also applies to The Joint List, a coalition of three parties — Hadash (a left-wing Jewish-Arab party), Ta'al (an Arab nationalist party) and Balad (a Palestinian nationalist party).

The alliance was formed in part to avoid splitting votes and to ensure the parties clear Israel's 3.25% electoral threshold. Together, Hadash and Ta'al currently hold five Knesset seats, while Balad has no representation in the outgoing parliament. In recent polls, the parties jointly hold at least seven seats.
Netanyahu vows citizenship crackdown over Gaza documentary

The CEC also banned two individual candidates from the joint list. These were the chairman of Balad, Sami Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian-Israeli politician and former member of the Knesset (MK), and Ofer Cassif, a Jewish lawmaker and current MK for Hadash.

The CEC comprises representatives from the outgoing parliament, meaning Likud is well represented. It reportedly voted 18-5 to bar Ra'am and the Joint List on Wednesday. The following day, the committee rejected a petition against National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party. Ben-Gvir recently drew criticism from Germany and many other countries for saying that he thinks "targeted killings should be carried out in Gaza" regardless of whether those people posed an immediate threat.

While a representative of the Supreme Court chairs the Central Elections Committee, the court will ultimately decide the ban after the Adalah rights group confirmed it would appeal on behalf of the parties.
Why are these parties banned?

Right-wing parties such as Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and Otzma Yehudit started petitions to ban these parties and individuals. A stipulation in the Knesset's basic law bans candidates who show "negation of the existence of the State of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state," "incitement to racism" or "support for armed struggle by a hostile state or a terrorist organization against the State of Israel."

Supporters of the bans argued that some of the parties' leaders had made statements or engaged in conduct that crossed those legal boundaries. In Ra'am's case, petitioners cited alleged connections between organizations linked to the party and bodies connected to Hamas, as well as statements by Mansour Abbas that they claimed reflected contradictory messages to Hebrew- and Arabic-speaking audiences.

Petitions against Sami Abu Shehadeh and Ofer Cassif similarly relied on past statements and writings that opponents argued amounted to support for positions that undermine the existence of Israel as a Jewish state.
Israeli govt. minister unveils Gaza mass emigration plan
What is the response of those banned?
Ra'am and the Joint List strongly reject the allegations.

Ra'am argues that petitioners failed to provide the clear and convincing evidence required under Israeli law. The party points to Mansour Abbas' condemnation of the October 7 attacks and his efforts on behalf of Israeli hostages as evidence that it does not support terrorism.

The rights organization Adalah, which is representing the parties, said "the CEC conducted an illegitimate political process aimed at persecuting ideas the majority does not accept, and it ended with the disqualification of all Palestinian representation in the Israeli Knesset."
The Joint List said the move amounted to an attempt to disenfranchise more than a million Arab citizens and accused the government of seeking to suppress Arab political participation.
Cassif struck a similar tone on X, when he called the decision "another nail in the coffin of the remnants of democracy" in Israel.
Has this happened before?

Not on this scale. While Israel's election authorities have previously attempted to disqualify Arab parties and candidates, the exclusion of all major Arab-led electoral lists at the same time would be unprecedented.

Balad, in particular, has been previously banned, before a Supreme Court ruling allowed the party to run after all. This happened in 2022, 2019, 2009 and 2003, often unanimously. Cassif's ban in 2019 was also overturned.
Since a 1985 legal amendment allowed such challenges from the committee, the Supreme Court has upheld only one such decision — against the ultra-nationalist Orthodox Jewish party Kach in 1988.
What has the reaction been to the banning of Arab parties from the Israeli election?
Many supporters of the bans argue that the October 7 attack and subsequent war in Gaza changed the political context.
They contend that statements or activities that may previously have been tolerated should be viewed more seriously after the Hamas-led attack and during an ongoing regional conflict.

Ahead of the CEC decision, Netanyahu's Likud party spelled out its backing for a ban. "There is no room in the Knesset for those who harm IDF soldiers and are unable to say that Hamas and Hezbollah are terrorist organizations," said a party statement.
Netanyahu suing Haaretz over reporting on Oct. 7 warning
Netanyahu is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza following October 7, 2023.
Responses from the Israeli center, meanwhile, have been divided.
Some centrist politicians have supported disqualifying specific candidates, while expressing concerns over excluding entire party lists representing a substantial minority of Israeli citizens.

Perhaps crucially, Israel's legal establishment has so far not endorsed the disqualifications. The office of Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara reportedly concluded that the evidence against Ra'am and the Joint List did not satisfy the legal requirements for exclusion, although it did support the ban of Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh.

Much of the media reaction has been scathing, with an opinion piece in the Jerusalem Post reading: "Israel has spent decades proudly calling itself the only democracy in the Middle East. Attempting to exclude the political representatives of Arab citizens, who make up roughly a fifth of Israeli society, is dangerous and fundamentally undemocratic."

Meanwhile, the Times of Israel lamented the CEC's back-and-forth banning process, saying that it's a "safe bet that on October 27, voters will be able to cast ballots for the Joint List and Ra'am," before adding that: "Given the unsuccessful track record of these disqualifications, coalition politicians may have been willing to play fast and lose with democratic rights in order to throw some red meat to their base and delegitimize the Arab parties — all while counting on the Supreme Court to maintain the status quo."

articles.title: New UK homes in flood-risk areas could become uninsurable, says Aviva boss
articles.summary: Amanda Blanc says flooding threat is ‘absolutely increasing’, as she also warns ministers over ‘kite flying’ before budget

blocks.text: The boss of Britain’s biggest insurer has said that homes being built now could become uninsurable in the future because they are sited in flood-risk areas.
Amanda Blanc, the chief executive of Aviva, said the flooding threat was “absolutely increasing”.
She told the BBC: “You’ve seen a very dry summer, and what happens if you then get heavy rain on very dry surfaces is you get more surface water flooding.”

She said 110,000 homes had been built in flood areas in the past 10 years, and if that continued, a further 115,000 new homes would be built in flood areas in the next decade. “That doesn’t seem to me to make sense. We need to think about where those homes are being built,” she said.
Blanc told the BBC’s Big Boss Interview podcast that England was “for sure” building properties that might become uninsurable in the future.

“If you think that there’s an inevitability of something happening, that’s not what insurance is, right? Insurance is a pool where you know there’s a risk that something happens for some people and not for others. When there is an inevitability, it makes it very difficult for it to be insured.”
She added: “It’s very well known where these flooding areas are. Let’s think very carefully about homes that are being built,” she told planners and housebuilders. “It’s dangerous.”

About 6.3m homes and businesses in England are at risk of flooding, according to the Environment Agency. It has said this could increase to about 8m, or one in four properties, by the mid-century as the climate crisis worsens.

If a property cannot get insurance cover or it is prohibitively expensive to insure because it is prone to frequent flooding, the homeowner would have to foot the bill, with knock-on effects on their ability to get a mortgage or sell the property. Some towns may have to be abandoned as climate breakdown makes many areas uninsurable, a Guardian investigation found last year.

Blanc said a lot could be done to mitigate damage, such as using bricks with self-closing air vents, having stainless steel kitchens instead of wooden furniture and creating plug points halfway up the wall rather than near the floor.
“You can do all sorts of different things to your property to make it more or less vulnerable to flood.”
According to Aviva’s research, more than a quarter (26%), or 101,657 new homes, have some risk of flooding now, and one in seven will be at medium to high risk of flooding by 2050.
after newsletter promotion
After the very wet and stormy winter in the UK in 2023-24, the Met Office estimated that such winters had gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events.
Blanc also called on the government to avoid policy “kite flying” before John Healey’s first budget as chancellor on 28 October.
Aviva is a leading private pension provider, and speculation about changes to pensions led to a jump in withdrawals in the run-up to the budget in the last two years.

“Effectively we saw in the last year 30 times the normal withdrawal from pensions that we would normally see, which is clearly something which customers may regret afterwards because once you take your tax-free lump sum out, you can’t put it back in,” she said.

Blanc has come under criticism over her role as BP’s senior independent director in which she led the search for a new chair twice in a year, after the controversial ousting of Albert Manifold. She will stand down next year after five years on the board.

She said: “It’s been a tough gig, right? There’s no doubt about that, and there’s been a lot thrown at BP. But if I look at it today and the combination of a new chair, new CEO, I think that’s a good combination to take BP forward … it’s time for me to move away.”

articles.title: Baste says he wouldn't have okayed GenCorp contracts if he had known VP Sara link
articles.summary: Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte said he would not have let the city government to award P33 million worth of contracts to GenCorp.if he had known that Sara had a business interest in it.

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 7:40pm

Davao City Mayor Sebastian "Baste" Duterte said he would not have allowed the city government to award P33 million worth of contracts to GenCorp. Industries Inc., if he had known that his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, had a business interest in the firm.
The mayor made the testimony on Tuesday at the impeachment trial of the Vice President as a hostile witness for the prosecution.
“I would not allow it,” the mayor said when asked about it by Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero.

The Vice President declared GenCorp. Industries Inc. as one of her business interests in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth in 2024 and 2025, but Mayor Dutete maintained that he wasn’t aware of his sister's declarations or stake in the company.
Earlier, private prosecutor Theodore Te asked the mayor if he is aware of the Constitutional prohibition on the President and Vice President having business interests and conflict of interest.
Duterte said he was aware.

Te went on to ask if the mayor was in the position to tell the Vice President that she should not engage with GenCorp. due to conflict of interest, but defense counsel Justin Gular objected by citing that the question was speculative, assumes facts and delves into hypotheticals.

Escudero ruled that Te should reform his question, prompting him to ask the mayor if he would have been in the position to call out his sister’s ties to GenCorp. as the head of procurement entity and someone aware of the Constitutional prohibition on financial interest.
Gular again objected to the question as being “speculative.”
Te argued against Gular by saying it wasn’t speculative and anchored on Duterte’s testimony.

“He has testified that he knows that provision. He is the son of a former president. He is the brother of a current vice president. And, Your Honor, I'm simply asking him if he is in a position to inform his sister,” Te said.

At this point, Escudero took over the questioning “to abbreviate the proceedings,” prompting the mayor to say he would not have granted GenCorp. contracts if he was aware of his sister’s links to the firm. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Senate ratifies bicam report on Philippine Geriatric Center
articles.summary: The Senate on Tuesday ratified the Bicameral conference committee report regarding the National Specialty Center for Geriatric Health, which is one of the priority measures of the Marcos…

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 7:32pm

The Senate on Tuesday ratified the Bicameral conference committee report regarding the National Specialty Center for Geriatric Health, which is one of the priority measures of the Marcos administration.
During session, Senator Risa Hontiveros moved for the ratification of the Bicameral conference committee report on Senate Bill (SB) 1509 and House Bill (HB) 6739.
Majority Floor Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri then moved to ratify and approve the report.
“Is there any objection? Hearing none, the conference committee report on the disagreeing provisions of SB 1509 and HB 6749 is hereby approved and ratified,” Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian.
Meanwhile, Hontiveros said the country’s health care system should be ready to address the needs of senior citizens.
She said the conference committee agreed to use the senate bill as the working draft.

According to Hontiveros, under the reconciled measure, the National Specialty Center for Geriatric Health, to be known as the Philippine Geriatric Center (PGC), will eventually serve as a national apex and coordinating center for geriatric health services.
While this has yet to be established and operationalized, the Evangelina Macaraeg Macapagal Geriatric Health Center (EMMGHC) will serve as the national specialty center for geriatric care.
Hontiveros said that when the PGC becomes operational, the EMMGHC will continue as a tertiary geriatric clinical referral hub with a formal referral and counter-referral system.
The PGC must be fully operational within five to seven years, according to the senator.

“Beyond these institutional arrangements, this measure is ultimately about our senior citizens. Gusto natin tiyakin na ang pagtanda ay hindi nangangahulugan ng pagkawala ng access sa dekalidad at espesyalista na pangangalaga,” Hontiveros said.
(Beyond these institutional arrangements, this measure is ultimately about our senior citizens. We want to ensure that aging does not mean losing access to quality and specialized care.)
“Ang mas mahabang buhay ay dapat sabayan ng mas malusog, mas ligtas, at mas dignified na buhay,” she added.
(Longer life should be accompanied by a healthier, safer, and more dignified life.) — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: 9,450 DepEd-funded classrooms unbuilt from 2021 to 2025 -- COA
articles.summary: The Commission on Audit (COA) found that the Department of Education (DepEd) failed to build 66% of the classrooms funded from 2021 to 2025 under the Basic Education Facilities Fund (BEFF).

blocks.text: The Commission on Audit (COA) found that the Department of Education (DepEd) failed to build 66% of the classrooms funded from 2021 to 2025 under the Basic Education Facilities Fund (BEFF).
In its annual audit report, COA said DepEd has long sought to address classroom shortages by partnering with the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) to implement BEFF-funded projects.

“DepEd failed to construct 9,450 or 66% of 14,267 classrooms funded from 2021 to 2025 transferred and implemented by the DPWH, primarily due to site-related issues, project modifications, approval delays, untitled school sites, and other noted deficiencies in the program components of BEFF,” COA said.
These issues, COA said, undermined the program's objectives of improving classroom ratios, ensuring adequate school furniture, upgrading electrification, and improving health facilities.
According to COA, DepEd transferred the implementation of BEFF-funded classroom projects to the DPWH, with a total of 14,267 classrooms targeted for construction from 2021 to 2025.
However, only 4,817 classrooms, or 34% of the total target, were completed within the five-year period, most of them in 2025, state auditors said.
The situation raised questions about the DPWH's absorptive capacity, given its difficulty in completing the physical projects, COA said.

In 2024, some of the reasons cited for delays included site-related issues, pending demolition and building permits, and unresolved environmental clearances. In the previous year, delays were attributed to requests for and approval of project modifications.

“These limitations should have been addressed through proper planning, as they have remained a persistent issue that ought to have been resolved years back, considering that the program has been existing since 2012,” COA said.
“[T]he spillover targets” also indicated that construction timelines were not enforced and that DepEd was unable to monitor project durations, the state auditor added.
Davao del Norte 'ghost' projects
COA also flagged “non-existent, abandoned and materially incomplete infrastructure works” in Davao del Norte amounting to P83,261,456.74.

The flagged BEFF projects included those under the Last Mile Schools Program, electrification of schools without energy, repair and rehabilitation of classrooms, and construction of school health facilities.
At Kamingawan Elementary School in Talaingod, Davao del Norte, COA found that a one-storey classroom building supposed to be constructed was a ghost or non-existent project.
“No structure was found upon inspection but paid up to 98.8%,” COA said.

At Duluyan Integrated School, also in Talaingod, a classroom building was supposed to be constructed along with a solar energy system. However, COA found that the solar energy system and school furniture had not been delivered.
The two projects cost P36,357,670.57.
A similar case was found at Dugayan National High School in Kapalong, Davao del Norte. The project cost around P25.61 million, but COA found that the building was largely incomplete and abandoned.
“Only the structural frame had been constructed,” COA said.
The project was already 98.9% paid, according to the state auditors.
GMA News Online has reached out to both DepEd and the DPWH for comment and will update this story once they respond.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Jaime T. Cruz: The business partner of Sara, Baste, and Pulong Duterte
articles.summary: Businessman Jaime T. Cruz also had close ties with former president Rodrigo Duterte, who once offered him the post of PhilHealth president and CEO

blocks.text: Businessman Jaime T. Cruz also had close ties with former president Rodrigo Duterte, who once offered him the post of PhilHealth president and CEO
MANILA, Philippines – Jaime T. Cruz is not just a business partner of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Cruz also has business ties to the Vice President’s brothers, Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte and Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo “Pulong” Duterte.
Testifying before the impeachment court on Tuesday, September 29, Baste confirmed that he knows Cruz and that they are business partners.
Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) records presented during the trial show that Cruz is president of Chinese Gen Bee Food Corporation, where Baste and Pulong are members of the board.

blocks.caption: Jaime T. Cruz: The business partner of Sara, Baste, and Pulong Duterte

blocks.text: Cruz is also a business partner of Sara in Metro City Chow Foods Corporation, and an incorporator of several other companies that Sara declared as business interests in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs).

blocks.caption: Who is Jaime T. Cruz, Sara Duterte’s business partner?

blocks.text: Rappler’s investigation also found that Cruz is among the shareholders linked to Gencorp Industries Inc., a company declared in Sara’s SALNs. The investigation revealed that Gencorp secured contracts from Davao City Hall while Baste is the mayor.
Cruz’s ties to the Duterte family also extend to their father, former president Rodrigo Duterte.

On October 15, 2019, then-president Duterte appointed Cruz as special envoy to China for trade and investments. Months before that, Duterte had offered Cruz the position of Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) president and CEO. Duterte eventually appointed Ricardo Morales to lead the state health insurer.

blocks.caption: Jaime T. Cruz: The business partner of Sara, Baste, and Pulong Duterte

blocks.text: Cruz and Gencorp president Kimberly Cruz were part of the business delegation that accompanied Duterte to his working visit to Japan in May 2019. It was during this trip when the Cruzes secured a deal to operate Karayama outlets in the Philippines, as well as an agreement granting them development rights for the Dohtonbori Okonomiyaki restaurant businesss in the country. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Estonia blames Russia for arson at defence factory that produces vehicles Ukraine has used
articles.summary: Estonian authorities said Tuesday they have concluded that an arson attack in mid-August on a defence company that provides military vehicles to Ukraine was an act of sabotage commissioned by Russian…

image.caption: Estonia's Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna, shown at the European Council building in Brussels on May 11, that Russia's charge d'affaires in Tallinn was being summoned to his ministry in response to the August arson in Tallinn. (Virginia Mayo/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Estonian authorities said Tuesday they have concluded that an arson attack in mid-August on a defence company that provides military vehicles to Ukraine was an act of sabotage commissioned by Russian security services.
3 Latvian citizens were arrested for mid-August crime and extradited to Estonia
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said that "such actions are absolutely unacceptable" and that Russia's charge d'affaires in Tallinn was being summoned to his ministry.

A fire broke out overnight on Aug. 15 at a building in the Estonian capital used by Milrem Robotics, but was quickly brought under control, the BNS news agency reported. On Aug. 17, two Latvian suspects were detained in neighbouring Latvia, and a third followed the next day.
The suspects were handed over to Estonia.
Milrem has supplied THeMIS unmanned ground vehicles to Ukraine.
The Estonian Internal Security Service said that it has concluded that the arson attack "was a deliberate and pre-planned act commissioned by Russian security services."

It said in a statement that "the modus operandi of the Milrem attack is consistent with other acts of sabotage carried out in Europe on behalf of Russia," adding that it "assesses that the attack is directly attributable to the Russian Federation."
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal wrote on X that "we will not be intimidated."
LISTEN | Victor Jack, Politico NATO reporter, on alliance tensions over Russia:
Front Burner26:05Why Russia has Europe on edge
Russia scoffs at accusation
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that "such statements are unfounded, ill-considered, absolutely not reflecting the reality, not containing any substantiation whatsoever."
"We cannot take such statements seriously, and we won't," Peskov said.
Moscow has been widely accused by Western officials of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilizing European nations.
The Associated Press has tracked around 200 incidents of sabotage and malign activity across Europe blamed on Russia since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022.
Concerns grow over Russia’s incursions into NATO nations

That includes organizing plots to set fire to warehouses, launching drones and trying to kill enemies abroad as well as stealing defense technology and carrying out cyberattacks on critical European infrastructure.
In a recent case that pointed to an escalation of such activity, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August using a drone laden with explosives.

"The proliferation of these hostile acts reflects a dangerous escalation on the part of Russia, which will only lead it into a dead end," Macron said.
The French leader expressed "full solidarity" with Estonia.

articles.title: LNG Canada to move forward with Phase 2 expansion project in Kitimat, B.C.

image.caption: A flare fires off from the LNG Canada plant in Kitimat, B.C., on April 11, 2025. CBC News has confirmed an announcement from Prime Minister Mark Carney on Tuesday will be about the long-expected final investment decision for Phase 2 of the LNG Canada project on B.C.'s North Coast. (Patrick Doyle/The

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

The multibillion-dollar LNG Canada Phase 2 expansion in Kitimat, B.C., is going forward, Shell Energy Canada says, in a move that could double exports of liquefied natural gas from the northern coastal facility to overseas markets.
Expansion of LNG Canada project could double LNG exports from Kitimat, B.C., to overseas markets
In a release early Tuesday, Shell Canada Energy — which holds a 40 per cent interest in the joint venture — confirmed the decision to move forward with Phase 2.
It comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney is in Vancouver on Tuesday to highlight what his office calls a "historic investment in Canada's energy industry."
His public itinerary says the news will be shared at 11 a.m. PT, followed by a 1:20 p.m. PT briefing on "new measures to protect Canada's oceans."
CBC News has confirmed the earlier announcement will be about the long-expected final investment decision for Phase 2 of the LNG Canada project in Kitimat.
The expansion project is expected to roughly double the production of liquefied natural gas from 14 million to 28 million tonnes annually, the companies behind the project say.
Why Canada’s LNG export expansion is far from a sure thing
The Canadian government says the expansion would make it the second-largest in the world, worth billions to the national economy.
Critics point out ramping up LNG production would also sharply increase the amount of emissions from natural gas production in British Columbia.

Environmentalists argue that reducing emissions carries more urgency in the wake of a federal report warning Canadians to prepare for a future that's 5 C hotter — which will lead to the disappearance of glaciers in western Canada and longer, more intense summer droughts, among other impacts.
Canada’s clean LNG pitch — and why not everyone is buying it

Still, the project has been identified as one of national importance under Carney, and has support from both the B.C. NDP and B.C. Conservative Party — who have each pledged to ramp up LNG production should they form government following the Oct. 24 election.
On the campaign trail Monday, B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson announced his plan to make B.C. an "energy superpower," promising to cut red tape in order to triple LNG production by 2035.

items: Canadians should prepare for a 5 C hotter future, report warns
B.C.'s two major political parties outline energy platforms ahead of provincial election

blocks.text: In response, the B.C. NDP argued the plan wasn't ambitious enough, and said it already has plans to have B.C. outpace Doerkson's projections.

The B.C. Greens, meanwhile, have called for a moratorium on LNG expansion, citing environmental risks and concerns about Indigenous rights, further saying that fast-tracking projects is eroding oversight and accountability.
What is the LNG Canada Phase 2 expansion?
LNG is made from natural gas, a fossil fuel often extracted in northeast B.C. and Alberta through a practice called hydraulic fracturing or fracking.
It involves drilling down into the ground and injecting a mixture of water, sand and chemicals into the ground to force the release of the oil and gas.
What impact will LNG Canada’s Phase 2 project have on local First Nations communities?
The gas is then shipped via pipeline to terminals, which cool it to about –160 C, at which point it can be shipped overseas for use as a fuel.

LNG is often referred to as "clean" because burning it for fuel causes fewer emissions than coal or oil — but that claim is disputed by some analysts because of the energy and destruction it takes to produce.
One of the known impacts of fracking is an increase in earthquakes, which have been felt with increasing frequency in B.C.'s Peace River region in recent years.

items: Gas flaring at LNG Canada far exceeds permitted volume, documents show
LNG Canada equipment problems, flaring violations detailed in report

blocks.text: LNG Canada is a joint venture company made up of Shell, Petronas, PetroChina, Mitsubishi Corporation and Korea Gas Corp.
Last year, its Kitimat plant shipped its first cargo load of LNG destined for Asian markets.
With files from Chris Corday, Lyndsay Duncombe and The Canadian Press

articles.title: COA flags DepEd issuance of vouchers to deceased students, dropouts
articles.summary: The Commission on Audit (COA) flagged the Department of Education"s (DepEd) overpayment of P938,000 in vouchers to students who had already dropped out or, in some cases, were deceased.

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 7:19pm
The Commission on Audit (COA) flagged the Department of Education’s (DepEd) overpayment of P938,000 in vouchers to students who had already dropped out or, in some cases, were deceased.
In its 2025 Annual Audit Report on the DepEd, COA flagged several gaps in the agency’s implementation of the Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education (GASTPE).
Some of these gaps included delayed fund utilization, mismatch between financial and physical performance, and weak controls in the implementation of the senior high school voucher program/
The COA said that this resulted in “undermining program effectiveness, efficient resource allocation, and delivery of educational assistance.”
COA found that there were 58 voucher program beneficiaries that were unverifiable that were either dropouts, transferees, non-enrollees, deceased, or absent without supporting records.
According to the COA, there were a total of 172,909 voucher program beneficiaries. Due to time constraints, the Commission took a sample size among these beneficiaries amounting to 5,507 students.

Out of this sample size, COA confirmed the existence of 5,383 beneficiaries through physical inspection, video and phone verification and review of their school activities. They were unable to verify 66 total due to being unable to contact them but 58 others were unverifiable for other reasons.

“The existence of 58 VPBs (voucher program beneficiaries) could not be verified for the following reasons: 32 had officially or unofficially dropped out, 12 transferred to other schools, 11 were not enrolled in the second semester, two were reported deceased, and one was absent during validation with no school records available,” COA wrote in its report.

For the two deceased students, COA recommended to the DepEd to include additional guidelines to govern cases of beneficiaries who passed away, as they only covered what would happen should a parent or guardian die. State auditors also advised agencies to strengthen monitoring systems.
There were also five voucher beneficiaries who were misclassified under wrong voucher categories, resulting in another overpayment of P14,710.
COA also found that there were incomplete and improperly maintained supporting documents for voucher redemption, including a lack of report cards and various certificates.
DepEd response
In a statement, DepEd said that it would act on COA’s findings on the voucher program.

“As part of its 5-layer validation, DepEd, through its co-manager of the Senior High School Voucher Program, Private Education Assistance Committee (PEAC), has completed its School Year 2025-2026 validation. Through this year-end validation, flagged cases are being reviewed and confirmed overpayments will be recovered,” the agency said in a statement.
“DepEd remains committed to ensuring that public funds are properly accounted for and used for their intended purpose,” it added. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: US ban on Canadian alcohol, dairy products and motorcycles takes effect as trade dispute escalates
articles.summary: Donald Trump's ban on nearly $1 billion worth of Canadian goods has come into force, further escalating a trade dispute between the longtime allies.

image.caption: Image: Ed White/REUTERS

blocks.text: The United States on Tuesday began banning imports of a range of Canadian products, including alcoholic beverages, some dairy products and motorcycles.
The move marks the latest escalation in the trade dispute between the two neighboring countries.
What Canadian products has the US banned?
The measures took effect at 12:01 a.m. EDT (04:01 GMT/UTC) and replace 50% tariffs that the US had imposed on some of the products since August.

The ban covers nearly $1 billion (€850 million) in annual Canadian imports, although that represents only a small fraction of the roughly $880 billion in goods traded between the two countries each year.
Affected products include alcoholic drinks such as beer, wine, whisky, vodka and rum, as well as non-alcoholic beer, molasses and some dairy products, including whey and protein concentrates.
The ban also covers Canadian-made motorcycles and mopeds with combustion engines larger than 800 cubic centimeters (49 cubic inches).
Why has Trump imposed the ban?
US President Donald Trump's administration says Canada discriminates against American dairy, vehicle and alcohol exporters.
How could Trump react to Canada-EU association plan?
The latest measures follow a series of retaliatory moves between the two countries.
Trump imposed 50% tariffs on around $20 billion worth of Canadian imports over the summer. Canada responded with tariffs of between 15% and 50% on an equivalent value of US goods.
Some Canadian provinces also removed US alcoholic beverages from store shelves.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the bans were a consequence of Canada's treatment of American exports.
How significant is the economic impact?
Jacob Jensen of the American Action Forum estimated that the ban covers $967 million in Canadian imports based on 2025 figures, with alcoholic beverages accounting for 87% of the total.
The previous 50% tariffs had already made importing many of the affected products uneconomical.
However, analysts warned that the move could provoke further Canadian retaliation and complicate efforts to renew the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement.
