articles.title: Impeachment court to prosecution: Present Sara Duterte bank records before Trillanes
articles.summary: Former senator Sonny Trillanes is among the prosecution's key witnesses in the Vice President's alleged unexplained wealth

blocks.text: Former senator Antonio Trillanes sits among House prosecutors during Day 31 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 29, 2026.
Senate Social Media Unit
Former senator Sonny Trillanes is among the prosecution's key witnesses in the Vice President's alleged unexplained wealth

MANILA, Philippines – Former Senator Antonio “Sonny” Trillanes IV may testify in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday, September 30, as one of the prosecution’s witnesses on the allegations of unexplained wealth.

On Day 31 of the impeachment trial, House prosecutor Terry Ridon sought to present Trillanes as one of the prosecution’s next witnesses, along with Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura, Kathy Florence Baldonado of the Register of Deeds in Davao City, and Marco Pineda of the Register of Deeds in Samal.
Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison questioned the move, saying it was the second time the House prosecution had suddenly changed the order of its witnesses.
“This means now that this would be the second time that the prosecution is changing the order of its presentation of the witnesses, just for this week,” Sison said.
“In fact, in the list of three witnesses disclosed yesterday, it does not include the name of former Senator Trillanes,” she added.
The prosecution’s move to present Trillanes drew reactions from some senator-judges, prompting presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero to call for a recess.

During the five-minute break, Escudero was seen discussing the matter with some senator-judges, who raised concerns about Trillanes testifying before the prosecution presents Duterte’s bank records. Escudero was also heard saying he could not prevent the prosecution from calling its witness.
After the recess, Escudero ruled that the impeachment court would not issue a subpoena to Trillanes but stressed that it “cannot prevent the prosecution from calling him as a witness voluntarily.”
“The court would like to remind the panel of prosecution to take in advisement the court will say: The cart cannot be put ahead of the horse,” Escudero said.

“It would be best as originally planned by the prosecutors, in their motion itself, to present at the very least the AMLC officer, and/or the bank officials or records given that the testimony of former Sen. Trillanes pertains to that,” he added.

Ridon, in response, said the prosecution wanted to present Duterte’s bank records “at the soonest possible time” but noted that their request for the admission of the evidence had only been recently resolved.
Sison then reiterated that the defense was withdrawing its objection to Trillanes’ appearance.
“We had withdrawn our objection and if they want to present former senator Trillanes tomorrow, then I think they should just do that,” she said.
In July, the Senate impeachment court granted the House prosecution’s request to subpoena the bank and financial records of Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.
The impeachment court also rejected the prosecution’s request for Duterte to admit to certain pieces of evidence in an effort to expedite the proceedings.

In his ruling, Escudero denied the prosecution’s request for Duterte to admit to “104 matters concerning respondent’s personal circumstances and former public offices, her spouse Manases Carpio’s business interests, and various Bureau of Internal Revenue and bank records.”

Escudero sustained the defense’s objection, citing Rule 26 of the Revised Rules of Civil Procedure, or “Admission by Adverse Party” that could not prevail over Duterte’s constitutional right against self-incrimination. He also ruled that Duterte was not required to answer the request and that her failure to respond could not be treated as an admission.
“The prosecution cannot shift its burden of proof to Respondent through the simple expedient of a Request for Admission,” Escudero said.

The court, however, rejected the defense’s request to expunge the request from the record. It said the unanswered matters would have “no evidentiary, factual or prejudicial effect against the Vice President.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Malaysia repatriates Myanmar migrants despite UN warnings
articles.summary: Malaysia has started repatriating about 1,500 Myanmar nationals, defying warnings from the UN and rights groups. Malaysia, facing an uptick in anti-migrant sentiment, says the program is strictly…

image.caption: Buses transported people to a naval base in the northwestern Perak state in Malaysia on TuesdayImage: Vincent Thian/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Buses accompanied by security vehicles, carrying migrants to a boat to be repatriated to Myanmar, arrived at a stadium near Malaysia's Lumut naval base on Tuesday.
Malaysia is starting the first phase a process agreed with Mynamar's military regime to send as many as 5,000 people back to the wartorn country.

Malaysia say the process is strictly voluntary, but the UN refugee agency and civil society organizations have voiced concerns about the security of those returning, saying they could face either military recruitment, persecution or detention amid the ongoing civil war.

blocks.caption: Ships were docked at the naval base, seemingly ready to transport the people to MyanmarImage: Vincent Thian/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What happened as Malaysia began the repatriation process?
The buses full of people arrived at the Lumuk naval base on Myanmar's northwest coast on Tuesday.
Two naval vessels and a hospital ship were docked on site seemingly ready for a naval transport.

Malaysia's Home Ministry had said in late August that the first phase of the repatriation would start in September. It said that the repatriation involved 1,476 Myanmar citizens identified by the Myanmar government.
Malaysia has tightened immigration enforcement in recent years amid rising local hostility against refugees, particularly ethnic Rohingya ⁠Muslims ​from Myanmar.

Myanmar's state media this month also cited the Foreign Ministry as saying it was working with countries to facilitate the voluntary return of verified displaced people in a safe and dignified manner.

blocks.caption: The identites of the people returning were not clear, though Malaysia had previously said that phase one of the returns scheme would involve almost 1,500 people in totalImage: Vincent Thian/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What's the security situation in Myanmar?
Myanmar has been in more pronounced turmoil since a 2021 coup triggered a civil war, with the military now fighting armed groups across multiple frontlines.

However, allegations of persecution and even ethnic cleansing of the country's Rohingya Muslim minority were prevalent long before the full-scale civil war broke out. To the same token, some of the country's regional conflicts and uprisings have been ongoing for decades.

The UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) says the current conditions "do not suppor the safe and sustainable return of refugees from Myanmar." It also said it had not been involved in agreements like the one struck with Malaysia.
UNHCR data suggests that roughly 193,000 refugees from Myanmar are in Malaysia, around two-thirds of them Rohingya.
Activist James Bawi Thang Bik said that based on accounts of refugees who had previously been deported, they could risk detention or forced conscription.
"We fear that they may be forced to fight on the frontlines of the conflict. For many it is akin to sending them to a death sentence in their own home," he said.
A wave of online agitation this year had amplified harassment and scrutiny of Rohingya in Malaysia.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said this month that he would invite Myanmar's military chief turned president, Min Aung Hlaing, for an official visit in return for accepting the Rohingya returns.

Myanmar's largely ostracized government, trying to portray itself as more politically legitimate five years after ousting former President Aung San Suu Kyi, is seeking greater acceptance among the international community.

articles.title: Who is Bel Zamora in Sara Duterte impeachment trial?
articles.summary: House prosecutor and San Juan Rep. Bel Zamora drew misogynistic remarks online after a clip of her cross-examining a witness during Vice President Sara Duterte"s impeachment trial went viral.

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 6:25pm
House prosecutor and San Juan Rep. Bel Zamora drew misogynistic remarks online after a clip of her cross-examining a witness during Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial went viral.

On Day 30 of the impeachment trial, Zamora conducted the direct examination on prosecution witness P/Maj. Jerikson Sangalang, chief of the Records Division of the Philippine National Police Firearms and Explosives Office.
Sangalang testified that Duterte had 22 firearms registered under her name.
In response to online detractors, Zamora brushed off the negative comments about her questioning style, saying her critics perhaps simply could not handle her sass and style.
“Siguro, they can't handle sass, they can't handle style. And well, really, I don't care if they bash me. I'm here to do my job,” Zamora said.
“Let's see. Yun lang (That's all). I mean, seriously, they should get a life,” she added.
Who is Bel Zamora?
Zamora is also known by her full name, Ysabel Maria Jorge Zamora-Jornada.
She is the representative of the lone district of San Juan City in the House of Representatives. She succeeded her father, Ronaldo Zamora, after winning the seat in the 2022 elections.
Zamora is a lawyer who was admitted to the Philippine Bar in 2009.
In 2004, she earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in Political Science from the University of the Philippines Diliman, where she graduated cum laude (with honors).
Before joining Congress, Zamora was a partner at Zamora and Poblador Law Office, where she specialized in litigation and handled family, civil, criminal and corporate law cases.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief for nuclear concessions – US politics live
articles.summary: President uses social media post to deny reports that he was willing to ease sanctions in return for ‘concrete’ steps over its nuclear program

blocks.text: Key events

items: 4m agoTrump to speak at America's 'golden age' event
17m agoTrump denies offering Iran sanctions relief for nuclear concessions

blocks.text: Trump to speak at America's 'golden age' event
Donald Trump will give a speech as part of an event celebrating America’s ‘golden age’ at 10am EDT.
The president is set to discuss a new tool, America.gov, which is aimed at improving citizens’ access to federal government services.

Other participants are expected to include SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, US secretary of state Marco Rubio, energy secretary Chris Wright, Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman and former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt.
The event takes place on the same day that Trump meets at the White House with House speaker Mike Johnson and artificial intelligence leaders.
Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief for nuclear concessions
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

President Donald Trump said he has offered Iran nothing to end the war, rejecting media ⁠reports that cited US officials saying ⁠he was willing to ​ease sanctions and release frozen funds for “concrete” steps regarding Iran’s nuclear program.
“This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.

Axios and CNN both reported, citing unidentified US officials, that Trump was willing to ⁠give Iran sanctions relief and free Iranian funds as part of a final deal on the condition that Iran showed “concrete progress” on the nuclear issue.
It comes as Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said Trump was ⁠a “big liar”, citing the ⁠president’s statements ​on ‌nuclear ‌weapons and other ‌issues.

“The ​enemy (US) knows that Iran ‌is not after ‌nuclear weapons,” spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said. “Their issue with Iran is ‌not its nuclear programme but rather its vastness, which they want to destroy.“

Trump has cited preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear bomb as a key goal of the war, ⁠along with ending its ability to attack its neighbours and creating conditions for Iranians to topple their leadership. Iran does not have nuclear weapons and denies it wants ​to develop them, but argues it has the right to a domestic ‌nuclear energy capacity.

Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian, in an ‌interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear program and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or ‌coercion”.
“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.
US and Iranian officials spoke separately with mediators on Monday as part of a renewed effort to end the seven-month war, according to officials of both countries.
In other developments:

items: Anthropic will caution investors that artificial intelligence could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity” in its IPO prospectus. As Anthropic prepares for an IPO listing, which could value the AI company at a monumental $2tn, it dedicated almost a third of its prospectus to discussing concerns around AI safety. The news comes as OpenAI has halted the release of its next AI model over safety concerns, the Wall Street Journal reports.

Trump will be on the campaign trail this week – hosting rallies in Durant, Oklahoma, on Thursday, Mobile, Alabama, on Friday and Vandalia, Ohio, on Saturday. The first two states are GOP strongholds, and Trump has pushed voters to turn out to the polls and pretend the president was at the top of the ballot this midterm cycle.

Pete Hegseth ordered the defense department to “protect and uphold the reliability of America’s voting mechanisms against external manipulation and disruption from foreign actors” in a 22 September memo. Hegseth’s order comes as concerns about artificial intelligence are on the rise, but also as the Trump administration has spread misinformation about voter fraud. In July, Trump accused China of interfering in the 2020 election, which he lost.

Andrew Bailey said he is stepping down as one of the FBI’s two deputy directors after just over a year in the role – a short tenure that unfolded as he helped oversee several of Trump’s election‑related investigations. Bailey was appointed in August 2025 to serve alongside Dan Bongino at a moment of sharp tension between the FBI and justice department leadership over the handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files.

Pope Leo addressed concerns about artificial intelligence and the war in Ukraine during a press conference onboard the papal plane today. Saying that concerns about AI are not “fake news”, the first US pope appeared to criticize Trump, who called concerns about AI a “hoax” during a UN address last week.

articles.title: Separatist group takes motorhome to northwestern Alberta to talk independence
articles.summary: The Let’s Talk Alberta motorhome makes a slow turn off Highway 2 into the parking lot of the Dunvegan Inn in Fairview, Alta., on a sunny mid-September morning.

image.caption: Neil Hart, a retired farmer and business owner from Fairview, said he supports Alberta independence because he believes it will bring more investment and jobs back to the province. (David Bajer/CBC)

blocks.text: The Let’s Talk Alberta motorhome makes a slow turn off Highway 2 into the parking lot of the Dunvegan Inn in Fairview, Alta., on a sunny mid-September morning.
The rig, which is running late, is met by a contingent of local people who stroll across the parking lot to meet the folks inside.

People involved with the grassroots pro-independence organization have been touring around Alberta ahead of the province’s Oct. 19 referendum, which will include a question on whether Alberta should remain a part of Canada or hold a binding vote on separation.
Neil Hart, a retired Fairview resident, came to meet the Let’s Talk Alberta motorhome.

Hart said he wanted to pick up more signs in support of Alberta independence and explained he’s helped put up the large ones along the highways that lead out of the town located about 115 kilometres north of Grande Prairie.
“When you’re headed towards Grimshaw, you see the one sign up on the granary,” Hart said.
“I have one on the south side of the road and there's another one just when you leave town, down on the side there, 8-by-16s. They look good.”
Hart, 68, said he used to work as a heavy duty mechanic, then farmed for 25 years. He also founded a company that provided mulching services in the oilpatch.

He said he wants Alberta to become its own nation because he wants to see younger generations have a chance at getting what he calls “real jobs, real careers” like he had when he first entered the workforce 50 years ago.
“I'm done. I'm retired,” Hart said. “It's my kids and grandkids. They need a chance.”
He said there was once plenty of work in the area but that’s changed. According to Hart, Fairview is turning into a “retirement town” and he’s urging his children and grandchildren to move.

“There's no jobs here. They got to leave,” Hart said. “I keep telling them, ‘Sorry kids, there’s no sense staying here. You got to at least get to Grande Prairie.’ Things are happening in Grande Prairie.”
Hart’s reasons for wanting to leave Canada were repeated by others who came to meet the motorhome belonging to Chris Scott, the founder of Let’s Talk Alberta.
People said they feel they pay taxes to the federal government and get little in return.

Others pointed to how federal elections appear to be settled before Albertans finish casting their ballots as evidence of how little influence the province has over policies that are crafted in Ottawa.
Few new faces at meeting
Fairview was just one of the stops that the Let’s Talk Alberta motorhome made in northern Alberta this month. Members of the group also held a town hall at a hotel in Grande Prairie.

About 200 people showed up for the three-hour event, which featured presentations from Keith Wilson, a constitutional lawyer and co-founder of the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, Benoit Trudeau, a self-described sovereigntist and author based in central Alberta, and Scott.
People milled about the room, chatted with each other and looked over the independence-themed hats, T-shirts, signs and bumper stickers for sale on the tables in the back of the room.

As a song called My Alberta Roots Run Deep wrapped up, Sandy Duguay with Let’s Talk Alberta welcomed people to the event. She asked how many were attending their first meeting and about 10 of the 200 people in the room put up their hands.
“Thank you for coming,” Duguay said. “I hope you find that your time was well spent by the time you leave tonight.”
When asked about the low number of new faces, Wilson said he wasn’t bothered by it.
“I don't use … [a town hall] as a gauge of support,” he said. “I use it as an opportunity to answer questions.
“And I use it as an opportunity to share with the people who do support independence ideas on how they can communicate and have open dialogue with others who don't.”

A new report on the financial cost of separating from Canada — completed by the University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy and commissioned by the Alberta government — was a point of discussion at the town hall. The report estimates the cost of Alberta separation could be as much as $170 billion over just the first five years of independence.
Scott took issue with the report’s focus on the costs of separation without describing the potential benefits that he called “priceless.”
“How many people in this room would have paid that much extra tax to know that when we go to the ballot as Albertans, our voices will be heard and we can affect the outcome of the election?”
“I would have been happy to pay it. This isn't about the dollars. The dollars are important…But this is about something so much bigger than that and nobody's talking about it.”
A recent report from the Wilson-led independence organization Alberta Transition Council estimated the transition cost would be $5 billion in one-time expenses.
A former Treasury Board senior manager said the ATC report ignored hundreds of billions of dollars in costs.
Former UCP minister sides with Canada

While Let’s Talk Alberta considers itself an educational society that encourages people to talk and listen to each other’s perspectives, the majority of attendees at the Grande Prairie event appeared to be in favour of Alberta leaving Canada.
Grande Prairie resident Mary Bourne, who runs a Facebook page called Republic of Alberta, said she’s been to several independence events.

items: On the road with pro-independence Albertans, one small town at a time

blocks.text: Bourne said she supports separation because she is tired of paying "income tax for Ottawa and getting nothing for it.”
Timothy Jordan said he plans to vote for Option 2, which would give the Alberta government permission to start the legal process to have a definitive referendum on leaving Canada.
He said he would prefer if Premier Danielle Smith could “work things out” with the federal government but liked having the option to leave Canada.
“Not necessarily separation, but separation if necessary,” Jordan said.
After the stop in Fairview, the Let’s Talk Alberta motorhome visited Grimshaw, Manning, High Level and La Crete.
Large pro-independence signs could be spotted along the highway. Signs of pro-Canada support were often less prominent like a Canadian flag attached to a fence or on a flagpole outside of a house.

The only pro-Canada message spotted by CBC was a handmade sign outside a house in Fairview: The words “Forever Canadian! Elbows up. F--- UCP” were scrawled in black marker on a piece of yellow cardboard.

items: As Alberta separatism referendum looms, flags become symbol of voting intention — and tension

blocks.text: The lack of open support for the pro-Canada option doesn’t come as a surprise to Travis Toews, the former Alberta finance minister under Jason Kenney.
Toews, who lives on a rural property west of Grande Prairie, is associated with Vote to Stay and Lead Not Leave, two groups in favour of Alberta remaining within Confederation.
Toews said many people in the region are not willing to talk about the issue as it can create divisions within smaller communities or even families.
He said some people tell him privately that they’re happy he is standing up for Canada. Others express their surprise that he isn’t on side with those who want Alberta to leave.
“I'm from rural Alberta, a cattle rancher, have been involved in the energy industry,” Toews said.
“I think they look at the boxes I tick and perhaps they're surprised that I'm not an ardent separatist.”

Toews said he understands why people were frustrated about the government of former prime minister Justin Trudeau. While he is still a committed conservative, Toews says he is optimistic about Alberta’s prospects under Prime Minister Mark Carney.
He said reports, like the one from the University of Calgary, show how high the cost of separation would be, which in turn would be absorbed by a smaller population base.
He said the message coming from the pro-Canada groups in the weeks leading up to Oct. 19 will be for everyone to get out and vote.
“This is an extremely important decision that we're embarking on as a province,” he said. “And it's fundamentally important that the vast, vast majority of Albertans participate.”
Divisive issue not talked about
Back on the northern Alberta roadtrip, the Let’s Talk Alberta motorhome was met by the largest crowd of the journey when it arrived in High Level, the penultimate stop of the day.
Helen Dyck was there to offer her support. She is strongly leaning toward voting for Option 2 on the separation question.
“You see people asking for food because they don't have enough. They cannot survive on one income,” she said. “What are these kids supposed to grow up with?”

items: As Alberta separation vote approaches, both campaigns are banking on voter turnout

blocks.text: Dyck said there is a part of her that wishes Alberta would remain in Canada but she doesn’t trust that the federal government would negotiate honestly with Alberta.

“The sentimental part that says I'm a Canadian, although I do believe I'm always going to remain a Canadian,” Dyck said. “But I think we can do better. We can do better than what we've done till now.”
Outside the group surrounding Scott’s motorhome, passersby on the south side of High Level mostly didn’t want to share their feelings on the referendum.

Mitch Brown was an exception. He said he is unhappy Albertans need to vote on staying in Canada and suggested the provincial government changed the rules to favour the separatists and allow the vote to happen.
“I'm thinking it's ridiculous it's even a conversation,” he said.
Brown added that he avoids discussing the topic with anyone but his wife.
Back in Fairview, Neil Hart posed for a picture with his daughter with the Let’s Talk Alberta motorhome behind them.
Hart says he finds people who’ve already decided they want to stay in Canada aren’t interested in changing their minds.
“There's really no sense talking to them because you know you're not going to get anywhere,” he said.
“It's people that are sitting on the fence I like talking to. They come around.”

articles.title: AI: Concern as Germany plans to double data center capacity
articles.summary: Germany is rewriting the rules to attract data center investment from AI companies. But local communities are becoming increasingly skeptical.

image.caption: A Google hyperscale data center is being built in Dietzenbach as part of a €5.5 billion ($6.2 billion) investment announced last yearImage: DW

blocks.text: The digital future is here, and it is unfolding in the town of Dietzenbach.
Google, EdgeConnex, and Maincubes, two US tech companies and one German, have each reserved a spotfor a data center in the small town near Frankfurt am Main.
Dietzenbach is a logistics hub near Frankfurt's airport, and home to 35,000 people.

The Frankfurt region, the center of Germany's financial industry, is one of the most attractive locations for digital cloud operators worldwide, and as demand for computing capacity continues to grow, more centers are planned for the region.
Locals worry about electricity and water usage

However, the news of plans for a fourth mega data center has been met with resistance by locals. The stacks of tens of thousands of computers in a data center need a high supply of energy to run around the clock. They radiate large amounts of heat and need cooling, which requires huge quantities of water.
The people of Dietzenbach DW met were worried about their water and electricity bills rising, as well as a higher temperature in their town.

"We want to know two things: What are the benefits for the local community here in Dietzenbach? And what are the environmental impacts?" said Dietzenbach resident Wilhelm Sauer, pointing at the four imposing chimneys rising from the EdgeConnex data center.
He and the other local activists believe that the toll the data centers will take on regional resources may not be offset by the limited number of new jobs announced.

Dietzenbach's mayor, Dieter Lang of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), however, is optimistic. He predicted that around 100 "high-value jobs" would come to his town through the Google data center.
He also expects it will benefit his city's coffers: "We expect a substantial tax contribution," Lang told DW.

But Tara Merk, researcher on Community Data Centers at the Weizenbaum Institute, is skeptical: She believes Germany can probably expect little revenue from data centers operated by US companies, "because the profits may be taxed elsewhere."
"Especially thinking about big tech companies — they're not going to be doing their taxes in Dietzenbach," she told DW.
Where will the next AI data centers go?
Data centers and lack of information
In August 2026, the German government launched a data centers registry listing energy consumption, water consumption, and energy efficiency measures for the data centers that are already operating.
But the list includes only around 300 data centers, far fewer than the estimated 2,000 data centers the government says are running across the country.
"Some companies report their smaller projects but not the big ones," Werner Neumann, board member of the environmental group BUND, told DW.

There is no official overview of how many data centers are being built or where. The civil society project Heisse Luft (Hot Air) has decided to fill these information gap, and has developed an online map of the planned data centers across Germany. The map is updated every day with information based on crowdsourcing from local communities.

"Theoretically, we should have access to this information," Tiziana von Witzleben, co-founder of the Heisse Luft initiative, told DW. "Maybe the German government doesn't have the capacity to [collect this information] and share it. But I believe it is on purpose, particularly [on the part of] big players like Google and Amazon. [They] are known to be very secretive about what they do. Because they know that if they tell people, they will get a lot of protest."
Unlike in the US, where a nationwide movement mobilized protests all over the country, protests against data centers in Germany remain a local community phenomenon.

In February, the local council of Groß-Gerau in the Frankfurt region voted against a €2.5-billion ($2.8 billion) data center proposed by a US operator, at least partly as a result of massive protests from the residents wary of heat waste, the daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reported.

In Maintal, another town in the region, an EdgeConnex mega data center faced intense protest against its plans to build its own gas-fired power plant. The €1-billion project is now searching for power alternatives in a region which is already hitting its grid limits.

blocks.caption: Many Dietzenbach residents view the construction of massive data centers in their neighborhood with concernImage: DW

blocks.text: The race for computational power

Germany is the largest data center market in Europe, both by capacity and number of sites, and the Frankfurt/Rhine-Main region, which includes Dietzenbach, holds over a third of the country's total data center capacity.
Its proximity to the Commercial Internet Exchange (DE-CIX) infrastructure in Frankfurt makes the region attractive for digital cloud operators.

To achieve its strategic goal of doubling data center capacity by 2030, the federal government, a coalition of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the SPD, has proposed amending the Energy Efficiency Act (EnEfG) that regulates energy consumption and climate protection.

The environmentalist Green Party questions whether the targets are based on real demand. The socialist Left Party, on the other hand, is skeptical of the expansion as a whole. Both parties oppose the government's plans to relax the rules to attract more data centers.

On the opposite end of the political spectrum, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) supports the expansion of data centers but criticizes the law promoting the use of renewable energy to power them.
Europe's quest for digital independence
Why are energy efficiency amendments controversial?
The proposed amendment would push back the deadline for operators to achieve renewable energy targets, and would relax requirements for the reuse of heat waste.
Despite this plan, Tara Merk still considers the push for energy-efficient data centers in Germany to be a progressive example in the global context.
But she is critical of the parts of the law that would give companies the right to declare that the data on the amount of water and electricity they use are trade secrets.

"This proposed amendment shifts the regulatory landscape very much in favor of operators," she told DW. "Having good data is needed to regulate, intervene, and build trust and acceptance within local communities."

"I think [lack of transparency] is ultimately going to foster more antagonism between data centers and local communities, making it harder for operators to expand or even keep their existing sites running the way they are," Merk warned.

Algorithm Watch, an AI watchdog, argued in a public statement that the legal changes the government is proposing are not about cutting bureaucracy, but more about appeasing US tech giants Microsoft, Google, and Vantage.
"German and European operators mostly have no problem with the current rules," Algorithm Watch said. "The amendments run counter to the government's own aim of strengthening German/European firms,"
This summer, the watchdog launched a campaign and collected 150,000 signatures against the amendments to the law, calling for the public reporting obligations of data centers to be retained.
The amendments were presented to the Bundestag in September. If the new law passes, the government hopes it will take effect in January.
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

blocks.text: Some evacuated residents reportedly return home although others are hesitant to do so
Residents in the Cotswold village of Whelford were told yesterday they were able to return home after being advised to temporarily evacuate to a local leisure centre.
About 85 households in Whelford were evacuated early on Sunday morning as a precaution due to the major police incident declared around RAF Fairford.
One local resident has since told the BBC that while most people have now returned home, others are hesitant to do so.

“I haven’t gone home as I want to wait until I know more about what the hell happened, as it feels super dodge to me,” the resident told the BBC, adding that police are advising people not to take any photos and to stay inside their properties.
A cordon remains in place around three vans which are being examined by counter-terrorism police near RAF Fairford, two days after the incident.
Here are some of the latest images from the scene that have been sent to us over the newswires:

blocks.caption: Police officers guard an area as roadblocks remain in place near the RAF Fairford airbase. Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Reuters
A journalist reports near the RAF Fairford airbase in Gloucestershire.  Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Reuters
An LTV (light tactical vehicle) operates at the perimiter of the RAF Fairford airbase. Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Reuters

blocks.text: Key events

items: 1h agoSome evacuated residents reportedly return home although others are hesitant to do so
2h agoWhat we know about the suspected plot at RAF Fairford
2h agoRAF Fairford incident 'clearly involves' foreign actor, US secretary of state says
2h agoI trust UK's police judgement on suspects, Labour's deputy leader says

blocks.caption: Jamie Grierson

blocks.text: Jamie Grierson

An MP and councillors representing the residents of the village near RAF Fairford who were evacuated due to the suspected plot have expressed scepticism and concern over the security response to threats made by Iran.

Roz Savage, the MP for South Cotswolds, said she had many questions about the circumstances of how the alleged plot was averted. The Liberal Democrat MP, whose constituency covers the military base, said she would be writing to the prime minister and the defence secretary with her concerns.

“Ever since it was first announced six months ago that RAF Fairford was going to be used as the base for US military airstrikes on Iran, I’ve been asking questions of the government about whether they can assure my residents, my constituents, of their safety,” she said.
“They had given that assurance. However, I feel that the events of this weekend do cast that into doubt.”
She went on: “Who knew what? When did they know it? Where was the ball dropped? What more could have been done to secure the safety and security of my constituents?”

There have been conflicting statements about who knew what and when. A farmer from Whelford told reporters she called police in the early hours of Sunday to report suspicious activity – which then triggered a rapid response.
But the US president, Donald Trump, also suggested to reporters the men had been under surveillance.

Tristan Wilkinson, a cabinet member for Cotswold district council and councillor for the Lechlade, Kempsford and Fairford South ward, which covers Whelford, said: “The American president indicated last night in front of journalists that there was some intelligence and that these individuals were under surveillance.

“If that was to be true, that they would have been allowed to get so close to the base and drive what was, at the time, believed to be bombs into residential areas of a small village, I can’t imagine the security services allowing that to happen.”

Iran has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target. But Iran’s embassy in London yesterday strongly rejected any speculation linking the country to the arrests of the five suspects near RAF Fairford.
The Guardian’s defence and security editor, Dan Sabbagh, has looked into the claims of a possible Iranian link to the alleged RAF Fairford plot. Here is an extract from his analysis:

double quotation markRAF Fairford is the European home for US air force bombers, essentially an American base on British soil. It has been used by the US in its bombing campaign against Iran, after the former prime minister Keir Starmer agreed to allow American strikes on Iranian missile launch sites in the war Donald Trump started in the spring. The base has also been a source of explicit interest to Tehran. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) issued a statement on 23 July, as the US carried out a 13th day of consecutive bombing attacks. It said that any bases used by the US to attack Iran, including Fairford, were “legitimate targets”… Tehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west over the past three years, as fighting in the Middle East has sprawled and expanded after October 2023, and particularly after Trump joined Israel to start a full-scale war on Iran in February. But while its propagandists make heavy threats about British military bases online, Iran’s actual threat is mixed.

blocks.caption: A US bomber and armoured car at RAF Fairford. Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The Guardian

blocks.text: What we know about the suspected plot at RAF Fairford

blocks.caption: Vikram Dodd

blocks.text: Vikram Dodd

Five men arrested over a suspected plot at RAF Fairford have been released on bail as police investigate why they were so close to the airbase in three vans with suspicious material in the back. The five suspects were revealed to be British men, all in their 20s and from London.
Their release on police bail suggests detectives believe it is unlikely they were on the brink of a mass casualty attack by exploding a bomb close to the base, sources said.
An Iranian link is still under investigation, as is whether any of the five were paid to gather in the village of Whelford, two miles from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire.

An initial examination of the vans led police to suspect they carried explosive materials, with assessments made as to whether they were viable improvised explosive devices. After the suspects’ release on Monday it emerged that no explosive material had been found.

The head of UK counter-terrorism policing, the assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, said the release of the men on bail did not mean the investigation was over and that they were subject to “stringent conditions”.

The suspects were arrested after a farmer driving home from a party spotted them. She said she believed they were wearing balaclavas and they ran away when her headlights illuminated them. She then called the police.
Donald Trump has suggested the plot was known to the US authorities. But British sources suggested the specific activities of the men were unknown. You can read more here:
RAF Fairford incident 'clearly involves' foreign actor, US secretary of state says

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, told Fox News last night that it was clear a “foreign actor” had been involved in the suspected plot at RAF Fairford, a British base that houses American bombers that fly missions against Iran.
“I have to be careful, there are some things I cannot say on the air for a lot of different reasons,” he told Fox News’ Hannity programme.

“Suffice it to say, that what happened, what almost happened, what could have happened, in the UK over the weekend, is a very serious situation. It’s one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor,” Rubio said, without providing evidence or giving further details.
“We are dealing with elements in the world and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally. We are always going to take that very seriously.”
Rubio said the UK authorities had been “very cooperative” in relation to the “serious incident” and have been “on top of it”.
He said “a lot of people are disturbed” by the fact the five suspects who were arrested on suspicion of terror offences were released on bail on Monday.

The US president, Donald Trump, went further in his comments, telling reporters at the White House he would not have released the suspects on bail. “We know everything about them. We would not have released them,” the president said.
Asked whether the case was linked to Iran, Trump said: “It might be.”

The five suspects – all British nationals from London in their 20s - were arrested in Gloucestershire on Sunday morning on suspicion of explosives offences and preparing an act of terrorism, with an Iranian link a key line of inquiry.

While the head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing, assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, acknowledged there was speculation over whether Iran was behind the incident, he insisted the force was considering “every possible angle”. The investigation is continuing and police are yet to establish a motive.

blocks.caption: Armed police enforce a cordon outside RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, England. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA

blocks.text: I trust UK's police judgement on suspects, Labour's deputy leader says
We are restarting our live coverage of the major incident at RAF Fairford after five British nationals who were arrested over the suspected plot were released on bail yesterday.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, suggested the suspected plot involved the hand of a foreign actor, and both him and the US president, Donald Trump, have expressed concern and surprise at the news that the suspects were released on bail.
Speaking at the Labour party’s conference in Liverpool this morning, Labour’s deputy leader, Lucy Powell, refused to provide details on what she said was a live police investigation.

“Bail and those kind of decisions are operational decisions for the police and they are not taken by ministers, and nor should they ever be. And I am very grateful and I trust our police and the judgments that they come to,” she told Sky News presenter Sophy Ridge.
Stay with us as we give you the latest updates on the investigation while enquiries continue.

articles.title: New electric bill format to reflect VAT-exempt system loss charges
articles.summary: In the new bill format, the allowable system loss charges are separately identified and excluded from gross sales for VAT computation.

blocks.text: September 29, 2026 | 5:52pm
This photo taken on May 15, 2026 shows electric meters of households in Mandaluyong City.
The Philippne STAR / Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) has adopted a new format for consumers’ monthly electricity bills to reflect the allowable system loss charges that were earlier declared exempt from value-added tax (VAT).

In a press release on Tuesday, September 28, the state’s electric power agency said distribution utilities are required to “clearly and separately” break down all the government-mandated pass-through charges in the new bill format.
The new bill format was approved by the ERC through Resolution No. 28, series of 2026, during a commission meeting held on September 16.
In the new bill format, the allowable system loss charges are separately identified and excluded from gross sales for VAT computation.
“The new format will make it easier for consumers to distinguish between charges subject to VAT and government-mandated pass-through charges excluded from VAT,” the ERC said in a statement.

The adoption of the new billing format comes after the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) formally removed the 12% VAT on allowable system loss charges in September as part of the government’s efforts to cut the electricity bills paid by consumers.
Standardized ‘other charges’
Aside from the new bill format, the ERC has also passed Resolution No. 30, series of 2026, to adopt uniform rates on “other charges” that distribution utilities may collect from their consumers.

“The new framework aims to make these charges more transparent, consistent with the applicable regulatory principles, and directly tied to the actual cost of providing specific services,” the ERC said.

Under the new policy, distribution utilities may impose and collect the “other charges” only on specific customer-requested and account-related services, such as connection, disconnection, and reconnection services.

It also formalized the computation for “other charges,” including only the direct labor, deployment and fuel, and replacement materials that were directly used for providing service. Other administrative-related costs, meanwhile, are excluded from the computation.

“For consumers, this means greater protection against double charging. Costs already recovered through ERC-approved Distribution, Supply, and Metering rates cannot be collected again from the Other Charges,” the agency added.
Late payment rules
Late payments were also covered in the ERC’s resolution, saying that they must also be identified as a separate item by the distribution utilities in the new bill format.
According to the agency, distribution utilities may only charge their consumers 2% of either the current month’s bill or the unpaid portion, depending on which is lower, for the late payment fee.
The distribution utilities were also reminded to properly issue a Notice of Disconnection to consumers in case of nonpayment.
The distribution utilities are given 90 days to adjust their billing and other systems.
“They must also make the uniform schedule of charges accessible through their bulletin boards, official websites, and other official social media platforms,” the ERC said.

articles.title: Spain grows fruit and vegetables for Europe — but it's running out of water
articles.summary: Spain's southern coast produces up to 25% of Europe's fruit and vegetables. But amid intensive farming, climate change and illegal wells, the water it takes to grow them is drying up.

image.caption: Spain's southern coast grows one-quarter of Europe's fruit and vegetablesImage: Bernat Armangue/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Donana National Park in southwestern Spain — one of Europe's most important wetlands, home to millions of migratory birds and threatened species like the Iberian lynx — is running dry. But rising temperatures and drought caused by climate change are only part of the problem.

The UNESCO-protected region on the Atlantic coast relies on an underground aquifer that's been tapped by hundreds of illegal wells. The reason: Europe's fruit and vegetable supply. Spain provides one-quarter of Europe's fresh produce, supplying colder parts of the continent with fruit and vegetables year-round.

The scale of water extraction in Spain is staggering: In 2016, WWF Spain estimated that the Donana wetland was home to over 1,000 illegal wells and more than 1,700 ponds illegally irrigating an area as big as 4,200 football fields.

blocks.caption: The 'sea of plastic' in Almeria is a massive expanse of plastic-covered greenhouses key to Spain's agricultural productionImage: Viajar24h/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: "It's gotten hotter every year. And the water dries up so quickly," one local resident in the town of El Rocio, just north of the wetlands, told DW.

"For me, day to day, the main issue is my animals," said another, hitching his horse up to a tourist carriage. "I have to draw water for them, but the well doesn't have enough water to provide it all at once."
Strawberries are lucrative — but come with a cost

The Donana area used to be royal hunting grounds, consisting of marshes and ponds. In the early 20th century, parts began to be used for dryland farming, agriculture in arid regions that relies heavily on rainwater.

But in 1971, Spain — still under the dictatorship of General Francisco Franco — declared the region's irrigation to be of national interest. The Almonte-Marismas Plan, named after the aquifer it tapped into, was part of a massive, state-sponsored effort to increase food production.

Authorities decided to bet on strawberries, which they called "red gold." According to calculations based on FAO data, strawberries can yield up to €150,000 (about $170,000) in gross revenue per hectare per year, compared to roughly €20,000 for potatoes or €15,000 for grapes.

But growing strawberries at scale also meant using a lot more water. Authorities handed out generous quotas and allotments, seemingly without considering how much extraction the aquifer could handle. Even those legal quotas weren't enough for the ever-expanding fields.

blocks.caption: Strawberries are one of Spain's most lucrative crops, earning up to €150,000 in gross revenue per hectare per yearImage: Adri Salido/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: Farmers turned to illegal wells and reservoirs to make up the difference. They built them to stockpile water, draining supplies from local residents and the UNESCO World Heritage Site next door.

"There was extreme drought and lack of attention from the administration," said Pedro Banez, of the Condado Water Users' Association. "And we found ourselves with a number of farms — or parts of farms — that fell outside the land classified as irrigable agricultural land."
Police, NGOs track down water thieves

The turning point came in 2019 when, following numerous reports of unlawful wells, a 2-year-old fell into deep, reportedly illegal borehole on farmland near Malaga and died. In the aftermath, Spain's Civil Guard police force created dedicated units focused on water theft.
Two years after that, in 2021, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that Spain had failed to protect the Donana aquifer, finding the country in violation of EU law.

Today, police and NGOs like WWF Spain track illegal extraction — near Donana, and other overtaxed agricultural regions across the country — using a mix of old and new tools. They start with satellite images of the region, comparing them against land rights maps to flag areas that appear greener than their legal status allows. Drones follow, giving investigators a closer look at where the water is actually coming from.
With Spain in drought, farmers drill illegal wells
Some wells are completely illegal. Others are legal but extract more than they're allowed, which requires closer, on-site inspection to prove.

Investigators check the flow meters that measure how much water a well is pulling. Tampering is common, often using a powerful magnet which disrupts the internal mechanism of the flow meter, allowing water to pass through unrecorded.
Farmers caught extracting illegally can be charged with crimes against the environment and fraud. Most face fines, but sentences can run up to five years in prison.
Spain's government, farmers tackle water misuse

In a bid to undo decades of overuse, local and national authorities have negotiated a €1.4 billion joint plan. The government has continued shutting down illegal wells, sealing almost 300 in the Donana region alone.
Officials have also started buying up farmland, rewilding it and turning it into protected areas, while setting up funds to create jobs in other sectors like tourism and renewable energy.
Spain's invisible war for water
Farmers, meanwhile, have had to change how they water their crops.

Many have switched to drip irrigation systems, where each plant gets its own individual dripper, paired with moisture sensors that report exactly how much water a plant needs. That cuts down on the overuse of both water and fertilizer.
Farmers have also begun planting less water-intensive crops and shifting their growing season to colder months.
Sustainable solutions to secure water
Spain isn't alone in confronting this problem. As economies mature, fruit and vegetable production starts being outsourced to places with cheaper labor, fewer restrictions and more sun.

Mexico, Brazil and Colombia grow food for parts of the US, while countries in southeast Asia export a lot of produce to China or Japan. Some countries in northern Africa, including Morocco and Egypt, also supply fresh fruits and vegetables to their European neighbors to the north. But, as in Spain, intensive agriculture has strained local water supplies.
Saving Europe's largest wetlands

Morocco has tried to turn the tide by using satellite comparisons to monitor irrigation and offering subsidies for farmers who switch to drip irrigation. In India, the government is trying to move farmers toward less water-intensive crops.
And in California, the US state has paid farmers to halt certain types of irrigation and introduced legislation to monitor and allocate water more sustainably.

Securing water, no longer seen as an unlimited resource, will increasingly be a challenge as the effects of climate change intensify. Addressing overextraction will take a coordinated effort from governments, farmers and the industries that depend on their water.
Additional research by Nicole Ris. Edited by: Martin Kuebler, Sarah Steffen

articles.title: Trillanes questions Baste Duterte's remarks over VP Sara's business interests
articles.summary: Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV on Tuesday questioned the statements made by Davao City Mayor Sebastian "Baste" Duterte over the business interests of his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 5:49pm
Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV on Tuesday questioned the statements made by Davao City Mayor Sebastian "Baste" Duterte over the business interests of his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte.

Trillanes said all mayors in the Philippines could enter into contracts with their siblings and simply "feign ignorance" after the mayor's remarks during the Day 31 of the impeachment trial of his sister.

"Kung pwede ‘yung sinasabi niya, lahat ng mayor sa Pilipinas, pwede makipag-kontrata sa kapatid sa kanila. They will just feign ignorance. So think about that. Ayun ang implication dito," the former senator told reporters.
(If what he's saying is allowed, then all mayors in the Philippines could enter into contracts with their siblings. They will just feign ignorance. So think about that. That's the implication here.)
The mayor appeared before the impeachment court to testify about his sister's alleged link to GenCorp Industries, a company stated in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN).
But Baste maintained that he has no personal knowledge about his sister's business interests.
"We do not discuss it," the younger Duterte said when asked by House private prosecutor Theodore Te.
Sara Duterte declared GenCorp. Industries Inc. as one of her business interests in her 2024 and 2025 Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).
The Vice President’s name, however, is not reflected as one of the shareholders of GenCorp. Industries Inc. in the company’s records submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission.

When asked how he felt seeing the Davao mayor in person, Trillanes, a staunch critic of the Dutertes, said: "Nakita natin, at least finally up close nakita ko. Sana nakita rin ng kababayan natin yung nakita ko. Whatever that is, saka na lang natin i-elaborate."
(I saw [him]—at least I finally saw him up close. I hope the public also saw what I saw. Whatever that is, I'll just elaborate on it later.)
Moreover, Trillanes said that he is hoping to testify on Wednesday in relation to funds and bank accounts as the impeachment court tackles the Vice President's alleged unexplained wealth.
However, the impeachment court has yet to issue a subpoena to Trillanes.
"I hope to testify tomorrow. So abangan na lang natin ‘yun," he said.
(I hope to testify tomorrow. So let's just stay tuned for that.) —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Sydney teen taken to hospital after falling from moving bus on northern beaches
articles.summary:
Transport for NSW, bus operator and Rail, Tram and Bus union investigate after incident on Monday evening

  • Get our

blocks.text: Investigations are under way after a teenage girl fell from a moving double-decker bus on to a busy road in Sydney’s northern beaches.
Emergency services were called to Manly Road at Seaforth on Monday evening after the teenager fell from the B-Line bus near the Spit Bridge.
She was treated at the scene for head and hip injuries and taken to Royal North Shore hospital, where a spokesperson confirmed on Tuesday she remained in a stable condition.

A Transport for NSW spokesperson said it was aware of the incident on Spit Road and that the bus had been withdrawn from service while an investigation by bus operator Keolis Northern Beaches and the department takes place.
“The passenger was treated at the scene and taken to hospital with minor injuries,” they said. “We wish the passenger all the best in her recovery.”
The incident has also been reported to the Office of Transport Safety Investigations.

On Tuesday, the Rail, Tram and Bus Union (RTBU) said Keolis Northern Beaches, “must urgently explain how a door on one of its B-Line buses reportedly failed” and that it was investigating reports from drivers that doors on the fleet had opened unexpectedly in the past.
RTBU NSW Tram and Bus Division secretary Peter Grech said private operator Keolis and Transport for NSW must “come clean” about whether warnings had been ignored.

“A 16-year-old girl fell out of a moving bus … on to one of the Northern Beaches’ busiest roads. It is horrifying to think how much worse this could have been,” Grech said. “She should have been safe on that bus and this was undoubtedly a highly traumatic experience for her.

“Drivers are telling us this may not be the first time one of these doors has opened unexpectedly. We are currently checking the circumstances, but Keolis cannot leave passengers wondering whether there were warnings it simply failed to act on.
“If a door can open while a bus is moving, then that bus cannot be carrying the public,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

Keolis responded to Guardian Australia’s request for comment on Tuesday afternoon with a statement confirming it was “aware of an incident that occurred last night on our B-Line service which resulted in a passenger falling from the bus near the Spit Bridge at Seaforth”.
“Our immediate thoughts are with the passenger and her family and wishing for a swift recovery.”
It is understood Bustech double-decker B-Line buses have been taken out of service, although Keolis and Transport for NSW have not confirmed which vehicles were withdrawn or when.
It has not been established when and how earlier concerns were reported to Keolis management, the response drivers received or what steps were taken to control the risk.
It is understood the union is seeking records from Keolis and Transport for NSW under the work health and safety act as part of its investigation.

articles.title: Danger zone: why war in the Middle East has landed the RBA’s inflation fight in tricky territory
articles.summary:
The Reserve Bank appears ready to push harder against inflation but it comes with a greater risk for the economy

The fight against inflation has entered a new, more dangerous…

blocks.text: The fight against inflation has entered a new, more dangerous phase.
For years, the Reserve Bank has been attempting, as gently as possible, to steer inflation back to its 2.5% target while trying to retain as many of the post-pandemic job gains as possible.
“That still remains the strategy,” Michele Bullock, the RBA’s governor, told journalists on Tuesday afternoon, an hour after the board announced the fourth interest rate hike for the year.
Unemployment has climbed by 1 percentage point over the past four years, sure, but at 4.6% it’s “still quite low historically,” Bullock said.
Other central banks have managed to get inflation lower, sure, but at the cost of higher unemployment, she said.
Yet there are signs that the central bank may be losing faith in this “slowly, slowly” strategy.
Bullock explained the RBA has been outside the 2-3% target range for six years now. That’s a problem, because households and businesses need to believe that inflation will fall again, one day.
“We came in [to the range] briefly in 2025, and then we’ve popped back out again. We are aiming to get it back,” she said.
But how to get inflation back under control “in a reasonable time”, when unreasonable things keep happening?
It’s the unending Middle East conflict that now looms as the biggest threat to the RBA’s careful approach to taming inflation.
As Bullock said: “When the Middle East conflict first started, everyone was sort of thinking, ‘Oh, it will probably not last very long’.”
“Well, that’s clearly not true. It’s lasted, and there doesn’t seem to be any end to it,” she said.
Fuel prices, fertiliser prices, transport prices are now all “permanently higher”.
“So this idea that they would go up and then come down again just hasn’t happened.”
after newsletter promotion

The RBA governor is worried that businesses are also coming to the same conclusion, and will start lifting their prices. That will make it even harder to get inflation back to target without a more dramatic increase in interest rates.
Bullock and her board have long made it clear they will “do what it takes” to get inflation back to target, a phrase they repeated on Tuesday.

After Tuesday’s announcement, a number of economists are betting the RBA will hike again in six weeks’ time, at the Melbourne Cup day meeting. Financial markets see a 50% chance of yet another increase next year.
All up, it sounds like the RBA is ready to start pushing harder against inflation.
That might be the right call, but it increases the risk the central bank will push too hard and, in Bullock’s words, drive the economy into a “dramatic slowdown”.
“Hopefully, in the next couple of years, when we get inflation back down, this will have all been worth it.”

articles.title: Lord Allan Velasco out of Philippines, BI confirms
articles.summary: No hold departure order or derogatory record prevented the ex-speaker's exit.

blocks.text: September 29, 2026 | 5:09pm

Image shows dismissed police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. (center) with former speaker Lord Allan Velasco and Vice President Sara Duterte. This is one of the photographs included with the affidavit Gracioso submitted to the NBI.
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — Fformer House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco has not returned from abroad with yet no cases filed against him, the Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirmed on Tuesday, September 29.
Velasco is among the subjects of the National Bureau of Investigation's probe looking into the allegations of Velasco's former security aide, Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.
The former Marinduque representative has not been issued a hold departure order or other derogatory record that would have prevented him from leaving the country,
Velasco cleared immigration controls without any legal impediment to his departure, the immigration bureau said, citing travel records. It, however, refused to bare more details.
"The BI cannot disclose further details concerning an individual's immigration records due to data privacy concerns," the bureau said.
A hold departure order is a court-issued directive that prevents a person covered by the order from leaving the Philippines while the restriction remains in effect.
"The Bureau remains committed to the consistent enforcement of immigration laws and policies while ensuring the proper protection and confidentiality of personal information," it added.

NBI Director Melvin Matibag separately said Tuesday that Velasco left the country on August 30 and had yet to return. Matibag said immigration records initially showed that Velasco was expected to return on September 14.

His departure therefore preceded the public emergence in late September of allegations by Gracioso, a dismissed police officer, involving purported cash deliveries to Vice President Sara Duterte he made for Velasco .
NBI looking into cash delivery claims

The confirmation of Velasco's whereabouts comes as the NBI investigates allegations contained in Gracioso's sworn affidavit. The bureau has said it plans to invite Velasco and other individuals named in the affidavit to hear their side.
The Philippine National Police said Gracioso had been detailed as a security officer or staff member of Velasco, although it did not immediately specify the period of his assignment.

Gracioso alleged that, on Velasco's instructions, he delivered suitcases containing cash to Duterte, former President Rodrigo Duterte and Davao City Rep. Paolo "Pulong" Duterte. He claimed he made more than 20 deliveries to the vice president totaling more than P2 billion and also alleged delivering more than P1 billion to the former president.
The allegations are being investigated by the NBI.
Velasco's camp has denied Gracioso's allegations, describing them as fabricated and inconsistent with verifiable events. Duterte has likewise denied knowing Gracioso or receiving money from him.

articles.title: Argentina's Milei threatens UK with international legal action over Falkland Islands oil project
articles.summary: A major offshore oil project is opening a new front in the Falklands sovereignty dispute, with Buenos Aires threatening legal action and sanctions against companies involved.

image.caption: Milei spoke at the UN General Assembly in New York days before threatening international legal action against the UK (FILE: 23/09/2026)Image: CNP/AdMedia/picture alliance

blocks.text: Argentine President Javier Milei on Monday gave the United Kingdom two weeks to halt an oil project near the Falkland Islands or face international legal action.
The potentially lucrative project has intensified the long-running sovereignty dispute as the islands prepare for oil production that could transform their small economy.
What has Argentina threatened to do?
Milei said Argentina would take the dispute to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg if the UK did not halt the Sea Lion project within two weeks.

"I instructed the Foreign Ministry and our legal teams to initiate arbitration proceedings against the United Kingdom for the illegal sacking of our resources through the Sea Lion Project in the North Falklands Basin," Milei wrote on X.
"If within two weeks the United Kingdom does not stop the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea," he added.
Argentina argues that Britain's authorization of oil exploration violates a UN resolution calling on both sides to refrain from unilateral actions while their sovereignty dispute remains unresolved.

blocks.caption: Port Stanley is the capital of the British-controlled Falkland Islands, which Argentina claims as the Malvinas (FILE: 07/10/2019)Image: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP

blocks.text: Milei has also threatened to bar companies involved in unauthorized oil exploration around the Falklands from operating in Argentina's oil and mining sectors.
His government has sent Argentina's Congress a bill proposing prison terms of up to 20 years for extracting resources around the islands without Argentine authorization.
Argentine authorities say they are investigating at least 60 companies and executives for possible violations.
What is the Sea Lion oil project?
Sea Lion is a major offshore oil field around 220 kilometers (137 miles) north of the Falkland Islands.
The project is being developed by Israel's Navitas Petroleum and Britain's Rockhopper Exploration under licenses issued by the Falkland Islands authorities.
Oil production is expected to begin in 2028.
The companies have rejected Argentina's objections, saying they hold valid licenses for the project.

blocks.caption: Britain and Argentina fought a 10-week war over the Falkland Islands in 1982 after Argentine forces invaded the British-controlled territory [FILE: 1982]Image: PA/empics/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The UK has also defended the right of the Falkland Islanders to develop their natural resources.
Why are the Falkland Islands disputed?
The Falkland Islands have been under British control since 1833, but Argentina claims sovereignty over the archipelago, which it calls the Malvinas.
Argentina invaded the islands in 1982, triggering a 10-week war with the UK.
The conflict killed 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British service members and three islanders before British forces retook the territory.
The UK says the islanders have the right to determine their own future.
In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters backed remaining a British Overseas Territory, with turnout of about 92%.
Argentina rejects the referendum and maintains its sovereignty claim.
