articles.title: New Princess Diana book 'not about settling scores,' says her brother, Charles Spencer
articles.summary: Almost 30 years after the death of Princess Diana, her brother, Charles Spencer, has written a new memoir about her life, her struggles and the royal institutions that were a big part of both.

image.caption: Almost 30 years after the death of Princess Diana, her brother Charles Spencer has written a new memoir about her life, her struggles and the royal institutions that played a role in both. (Sean Brocklehurst/CBC)

blocks.text: Charles Spencer says his new book about his sister, the late Princess Diana, is not an attempt to get revenge on his former in-laws, the British Royal family.
"It's not about settling scores," Spencer, a historian, journalist and the 9th Earl Spencer, told CBC Radio's The Current.
"I could have written something much more devastating," he said. "This was the considered version that I thought, 'Yeah, whatever's in here, needs to be in, to give the full story of Diana's life."
The book, Swan Song: Diana, my sister, has prompted a barrage of international headlines over its claims, including that the then-Prince Charles sounded "giddily elated" when Diana died.
But Spencer said he wrote it in part because he's been inundated with interview requests ahead of the 30th anniversary of her death next year.
"I began to think, 'Well, if everyone wants to know the truth, I think it's time for that,' " he said.
Spencer sat down with The Current's Matt Galloway to discuss the book, and his sister's legacy.
Charles 'upbeat' in call after Diana's death

Diana was arguably the most famous woman in the world after she married Charles in 1981, and gave birth to two sons, William and Harry. But after a tumultuous marriage, the royal couple separated in 1992, finalizing their divorce in 1996.
After leaving the Royal Family, she became a style icon and philanthropist, leading campaigns to clear landmines and challenge stigma around HIV and AIDS.
But she increasingly strained under the glare of the tabloid media and died in a car crash in Paris in 1997, after a high-speed chase while being pursued by paparazzi.

In the book, Spencer claims that Charles sounded "giddily elated" in a phone call after Diana died. Spencer said he'd already received calls from many people wishing to express their shock and offer their condolences.
"He just sounded completely different to everyone else … sort of buoyant … upbeat," he said.
"It was so jarring, particularly among all the sea of other voices."
Earl Spencer says Charles 'went nuts' in call after Diana's death

Spencer also wrote that he argued with Charles in the days following Diana's death, over palace plans for Princes William and Harry to walk behind their mother's coffin in the funeral cortege. Spencer said he told Charles it would be an ordeal Diana would not have wanted her sons to endure.
"He went nuts and started screaming and shouting," Spencer said. "And then he pulled himself together, I thought — and then, he said, 'We'll forget her soon enough.' "
"I was stunned. And I went, 'I can't believe you just said that,' and hung up on him."
Buckingham Palace responded to the allegations earlier this month.

"While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," the palace said in a statement.
Spencer described the statement as "classic gaslighting."
"They're trying to say maybe it's grief, maybe it was a long time ago, but they're trying to put a question mark over my reliability. It's a tactic, but I don't think it's worked for them."
Earl Spencer calls Buckingham Palace’s response to his book ‘classic gaslighting’
Funeral procession was 'exhausting emotionally'
Princes William and Harry did walk behind their mother's coffin, alongside Spencer and other family members — with thousands of people thronged on either side of their route.
In the book, Spencer describes it as walking through a tunnel of grief, where the reactions of the crowd kept shifting.

"We could walk for 100 metres and it would be silent, you could just hear sobs. And then [further on], people wailing, like it's a biblical thing, a sort of wailing and gnashing of teeth," he told Galloway, adding that some people screamed out their love for Diana and for her two sons.
"For over half an hour, we were just walking with this crashing in from all sides," he said, describing it as emotionally exhausting.
Some solace came from the late Prince Philip, the late Queen Elizabeth's husband.
"He was very much there for his grandsons, and he took control of it," Spencer said. "He said to the other four of us, the most important thing is to just keep looking ahead."
Spencer hid eulogy from palace
Diana's funeral took place at Westminster Abbey on Sept. 6, 1997. Spencer delivered a eulogy that spoke of her talents, while also delivering sharp criticism of the press and paparazzi.

But at a rehearsal the day before the funeral, he was asked to read his speech for a microphone check in the Abbey. As he climbed the steps to the lectern, "a handful of people, not that many, appeared out of the shadows," he said.
"An alarm went in my brain thinking, 'Hey, this is odd.' And then in that moment I realized they were probably listening … that they were gonna vet it and perhaps veto it," he told CBC.
So Spencer said he'd forgotten the speech at home, and instead started to read from a prayer book.
"I'd hardly read a word when they went, 'That's OK.' And then at that moment I realized that I'd saved the speech."
More than two billion people watched Diana's funeral, with Spencer's eulogy prompting a standing ovation from the crowds watching on screens outside.

But in the days before the funeral, Spencer discovered that the palace had invited the editors of Britain's tabloid newspapers. Believing they had hounded Diana during her lifetime, Spencer called each editor individually.
"I said just please don't come, it's totally inappropriate. Given the circumstances of Diana's death, it's obviously not right that you attend this funeral," he told The Current.
"That really did upset them, but it shouldn't have. They shouldn't have accepted."
Earl Spencer says ‘vicious’ treatment of Harry and Meghan not OK
Harry and Meghan suffering same demonization
Spencer thinks his sister suffered immensely under the glare of the paparazzi, who would provoke her to get the photographs they wanted.
"They would call her the worst words in the world, take a picture and then say, 'Look at her looking upset, she must be deranged or she's mentally unstable,' " he said.
"I mean that is so appalling. As a brother it still makes my blood boil."

items: Why Prince Harry and Meghan face more challenges after their return to the U.K.
The 'shockwaves' of Prince Harry and Meghan's return to the U.K.

blocks.text: He thinks things have improved since the 1990s, but still sees people being demonized in the public eye, including his nephew, Prince Harry, and his wife Meghan, Duchess of Sussex.
"I'm not saying Diana or Harry or Meghan or whatever are perfect people, but they're people. And I do think the public have to remember this," he said.
"Sometimes, I see these appalling comments under newspaper articles from people, and I think those people should be ashamed of piling in on a witch hunt."
Diana the sister, Diana the superstar
On the day she married Charles, Diana "emerged from Saint Paul's Cathedral as a global superstar," Spencer said.
"I certainly didn't see that coming. I mean, she's just my big sister," he said, adding that because he was just 17 at the time, he was "a typical, self-centred, hormonal teenager."

items: What is the truth about Diana? Her brother offers his view, ‘once and for all’
Jane Darville fought stigma at height of AIDS crisis, with a little help from Princess Diana

blocks.text: In the years that followed, he learned to focus on his original connection with his sister, by "cutting that away from the Princess Di or Lady Di of the media's imagination and semi-invention."

That wasn't always easy. He remembers one dinner where they met with old friends, who were suddenly sycophantic, having been swayed "into treating her as someone different to the Diana they'd always known."
He said he walked home that night puzzled by the shift and wondering what to do.
"I realized, my job as her brother from that point on was to always just be true, be the same brother," he said.
"And if that meant that sometimes she didn't like what I [said], then it was still good for her, I hope."

articles.title: Tessa Virtue says taking on dance without skates is 'terrifying' and 'invigorating'
articles.summary: Tessa Virtue, the three-time Olympic champion ice dancer, will make her stage debut — without skates — in a new solo contemporary dance performance at the Fall For Dance North Festival in Toronto.

image.caption: Tessa Virtue, left, and choreographer Alyssa Martin during rehearsal at a studio space at Meridian Hall in Toronto on Sept. 28. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Tessa Virtue, the three-time Olympic champion ice dancer, will make her stage debut — without skates — in a new solo contemporary dance performance at the Fall For Dance North Festival in Toronto.
Olympic champion makes her dance debut in a new solo performance at Toronto dance festival
Tessa Virtue finds freedom and fear in return to dance
For most of her life, Tessa Virtue has built a career on control.
On the ice, she learned to find the precise balance point on a blade, trust a partner implicitly and make even the most difficult movements look effortless.

With Scott Moir, she transformed ice dance into storytelling built on speed, precision, trust and emotion. Together, they won three Olympic gold medals, three world titles and a permanent place in Canadian sports history.

items: Tessa and Scott reflect on their partnership 5 years after retirement
Virtue and Moir lead star-studded group of inductees into Canada's Sports Hall of Fame

blocks.text: Now, Virtue is being asked to do something that runs against much of what made her an elite athlete: lose her balance, embrace uncertainty and perform alone.

Her new contemporary dance solo, choreographed by Alyssa Martin, premieres Oct. 15 at the Fall for Dance North Festival in Toronto, where Martin is the artist-in-residence. It is Virtue's first major performance on a stage rather than in a rink — and a return to the art form she first loved.
Virtue says she feels excited and honoured to be asked to participate, but the opportunity has also brought mixed emotions.
"It feels very much like returning to something and also utterly terrifying, but I think that's what's making this feel kind of electrifying and invigorating," she told CBC News.
Why Scott Moir won't be Tessa Virtue's dance partner this time
Dance was Virtue's first love. She began at three, and dance studios became places of comfort whenever skating took her away from home — first at 13, then again when she moved to Michigan at 15.
But returning to dance has not meant simply transferring the skills she developed as an ice dancer onto a stage. Virtue says the two forms demand fundamentally different relationships with the body.

"On the ice, I was technically proficient at finding the balance point on my blade," Virtue said. "In dance, it turns out the momentum and energy that you can create on stage comes from actually tipping off axis and playing with the recovery of that."
For Virtue, that has meant moving away from the controlled perfection demanded by elite skating and toward something looser, riskier and more exposed.
She describes the process as embracing "the messiness and the raw feelings" — a shift she calls cathartic for her nervous system.
The solo also marks the first time in years that Virtue has performed alone. She even asked Moir whether he wanted to join her for a duet.
"He's busy coaching his other athletes and he has a life," she said, laughing.

Instead, Virtue found a new kind of partnership in the rehearsal room and through the wider dance community. Martin says she was drawn to Virtue's performance style long before they began working together.

"There's something that she brings to her performances that is just so authentic and open and generous," Martin told CBC News. "That generosity is not quiet at all. It's quite loud and just so overflowing with this warmth and this power."
The work is set to Céline Dion's It's All Coming Back to Me Now, a song chosen by Martin, who says she immediately knew Virtue could bring power to it.
Robert Binet, Fall for Dance North Festival's artistic director and co-CEO, says the collaboration is exactly the kind of artistic risk the festival hopes to encourage.
"It's a real adventure in bringing two artists who have had very different artistic upbringings and careers together, but who share this absolute love of dance," Binet said.
He hopes audiences will see Virtue in unfamiliar territory, and recognize that the qualities that made her an extraordinary ice dancer can travel beyond the rink.

"People know her as the most extraordinary ice dancer in the world," he said. "I really want people to see that if you love ice dance, you also love dance, and it's just about people moving to music and sharing parts of themselves with you."
Virtue, meanwhile, hopes audiences remain open to whatever they feel.
"You don't need to know the vocabulary of dance," she said. "You just need to enjoy and remain open to feeling something."
As for what comes next, Virtue says she's leaving the door open.
"While I might not always feel confident in taking on a challenge, I can always be courageous," she said.
Virtue's solo premieres Oct. 15 at Fall for Dance North in Toronto. The festival runs Oct. 15-25.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Christine Pagulayan is a Toronto-based producer and writer with CBC News, currently with the Entertainment unit. She has worked in various roles at CBC News Network and The National. She has also worked as a multiplatform reporter in Toronto, Winnipeg, Halifax and Moncton. You can reach her at christine.pagulayan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Ontario investigates condo management company as investors scramble, tenants left confused
articles.summary: Ontario's condominium management regulator is investigating SIREG Management after the company told investors it could no longer guarantee rent payments, leaving some owners scrambling to collect…

image.caption: Many of units in this cluster of apartments on Kipps Lane have been converted to condos and sold to investors who rent them out. (Andrew Lupton/CBC News)

blocks.text: London

Ontario's condominium management regulator is investigating SIREG Management after the company told investors it could no longer guarantee rent payments, leaving some owners scrambling to collect rent directly from tenants.
SIREG Management says it can no longer guarantee rent payments for investors in about 1,800 condo units

The investors for many of the 21 buildings SIREG operates have been left scrambling, with some showing up to units to collect rents from tenants in person. The company runs about 1,800 condo units across Ontario including Sarnia, Kitchener, Welland, North Bay and London's Kipps Lane.
Some tenants at Kipps Lane in London told CBC News they didn't know they were living in investor-owned condo units because their rent cheques went to SIREG.

A handful of investors who spoke to CBC News said they were generally happy with their investments until last week when the company dropped a bombshell, telling them they could no longer guarantee rent payments.

In a statement to CBC News, the Condominium Management Regulatory Authority of Ontario (CMRAO) confirmed they've received five complaints about SIREG and have "commenced investigations into the matters raised."

items: 'Liquidity challenges' at SIREG Management leave Ontario condo investors scrambling
Why things can get tricky when apartment buildings are 'condominiumized'

blocks.text: The CMRAO licenses condo managers, operates a public registry of condo management boards and can issue penalties in cases in which a tribunal determines there have been violations of its code of ethics.
LISTEN | Investors scrambling as condo manager hits 'liquidity challenges':
Afternoon Drive7:54Challenges at Ontario company leaves condo investors scrambling
Pitched as hands-off investments

Since the early 2010s SIREG has bought older rental buildings, converted them to condos and sold them to investors seeking rental income. Under the arrangement SIREG was to manage the properties, collect rents and pay the condo board management fees. After those costs were covered, investors were paid monthly rent dispersals.

SIREG condos were pitched as hands-off investments, allowing buyers to become landlords at a low entry price with no need to deal with tenants. Investors had no information about their tenants, including contact information.

The same statement said SIREG president Todd C. Slater had stepped away for health reasons. Another statement said Reflect Advisors has been appointed to lead the company's management team and to "preserve value for the company and its stakeholders."
Amid the turmoil some condo owners have started to approach tenants in an attempt to collect rent themselves. Other owners are sharing information and contact information on new Facebook groups.
Calls to SIREG for comment on Monday went unanswered.
'Shocked' by state of disrepair
Patrick D’Sa owns two condos in two SIREG-run buildings in the 700-block of Kipps Lane in London. D'Sa, who lives in Toronto, visited the units he owned for the first time on Monday.
He told CBC News he was shocked by the buildings' overall state of disrepair. He said he understands why tenants are feeling uneasy when approached by landlords they don't know.
He said he's taking a soft approach in his first discussion with tenants.

"I don't want to scare people and they don't know me from boo," said D'Sa. "I'm giving them a letter showing them that I am the owner and if they could contact me, we'll talk about things going forward. They shouldn't feel afraid that they're going to lose their home."
D'Sa said he's concerned about the overall financial health of the condo board managing the Kipps Lane buildings. Most condo boards are composed of owners who live in the buildings.

According to information on the CMRAO registry, directors of the boards that manage 756 and 754 Kipps Ln. each have three directors: Todd Slater, his wife Sheila Vos Slater and Michael Sackmann. When contacted by CBC News, Sackmann said he didn't want to comment and said his employment at SIREG ended last week.
D'Sa said some investor-owners are trying to organize and force condo board meetings with enough votes to oust SIREG from control.
Tenants 'shocked' when owners turn up
Meanwhile, some tenants say they are uncomfortable being approached by people they don't know and being asked to pay rent directly to them.
Alexandra Stuart, who lives at 756 Kipps Lane, said she hasn't been approached by the owner of her unit, but many of her neighbours have.
"Tenants are shocked that their units are owned," Stuart said.
She said tenants understand that investors need to collect rent to cover their mortgages and other expenses, but are concerned about how the sudden change is being handled.
"We understand the owners' plight, they need to collect their rents and pay their mortgages but our legal obligation is to SIREG," she said.
"Threatening tenants with new leases and 'Pay us now' is making us angry. For the investors it was supposed to be hands off, now they're at our doors."

The situation has left both tenants and investors trying to understand what happens next, including who is responsible for collecting rent, paying bills and managing the buildings as the CMRAO investigates.

articles.title: Canada led a 2022 deal to protect the world's nature. Has there been progress since then?
articles.summary: Canada helped land a global agreement to protect nature in 2022. A new assessment shows how successful it's been.

image.caption: The COP15 UN conference in Montreal in 2022 led to a historic global agreement on protecting nature. (Paul Chiasson/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: During a snowy Montreal winter in 2022, Canada welcomed over 180 UN member countries to negotiate an ambitious new agreement to protect nature. The world’s biodiversity was in an unprecedented crisis — with more than one million species facing the threat of extinction, leaders were finally waking up to how close ecosystems were to collapsing.

Steven Guilbeault, then-minister of environment, helped wrangle a consensus and establish a new goal of protecting 30 per cent of global land and oceans by 2030, meant to halt the mass extinction. These spaces would be protected for the long-term goal of conservation, with human activities like fishing and mining banned or heavily restricted.
The agreement also included a promise to help lower-income countries with funding: money to establish and manage these protected spaces.
“That was the compromise in Montreal,” said Guilbeault, while on his way back from Climate Week NYC, held alongside the UN General Assembly to bring together climate advocates and policymakers.
“Those people who wanted more ambition had to agree to commit to more funding, and those who wanted more funding had to agree to more ambition.”
LISTEN | World leaders discuss climate in New York:
The Early Edition7:14Climate Week taking place to coincide with UN General Assembly in New York

But that funding is now the main roadblock in reaching the goals of the Montreal agreement. A new assessment report released in New York this week projected that, based on commitments made so far, just 27 per cent of lands and only 12 per cent of oceans will be protected by 2030.

“We have a reasonable shot of reaching our terrestrial targets. We won't be at 30 per cent [but] we'll be close to it,” said Guibeault, who resigned as an MP earlier this year because of the Carney's government's climate rollbacks.
“That's certainly something that should give us comfort. But on oceans protection, there is a lot more work that needs to be done.”
The assessment also comes as Canada, the country where the 2022 deal was made, has shifted its priorities toward fast-tracking resource projects, putting it behind on its own climate targets.
Rich countries need to put up more money: report

Speeding up nature protection and reaching goals will primarily involve increasing funding, according to the assessment, led by international advocacy groups Campaign for Nature and Together for the Ocean.

The Montreal agreement included a target of $30 billion US per year in international financing for biodiversity conservation in developing nations, of which about $6 billion US of that target is needed specifically to establish protected areas on land and in the oceans.

But international finance has only reached $1.1 billion US per year, it said. This money is supposed to flow from higher-income countries like Canada and Japan to developing ones, meant to create parks and conserved areas, pay for programs like park rangers and support communities and institutions in those regions.
“More money is flowing to countries in the Global South than before, but it's still not enough," Guilbeault said.

The report also said most of the funding is coming from just five major sources: the World Bank; the European Union; Germany; the Global Environment Facility, a multilateral development fund; and the non-profit Rainforest Trust.
The report warned that changes by even one of these funders could jeopardize the total amount.
Still, it also highlighted successes: More than 50 countries already report terrestrial coverage of at least 30 per cent. To date, 20 per cent of lands and 10 per cent of oceans have been protected.

And more help is on the way. This week, Canada ratified the High Seas Treaty, a new global agreement to regulate the oceans and seas currently outside of national jurisdictions. With the majority of world nations now signed on, experts say it will be easier to designate large areas of ocean as protected.
Oceans protection gets a boost

Until now, 101 countries have ratified the High Seas Treaty. Opened to signatures in 2023, it forms a new kind of international law to govern the oceans, such as new mechanisms to propose conserved areas, to fight climate change and to safeguard marine resources like fisheries that support billions of people.
The treaty has officially come into force last January and its first gathering is set for January 2027.

Canada is leading in ocean protection, as well, by hosting the Our Ocean Conference in Halifax in April. Prime Minister Mark Carney also committed $82 million toward monitoring the ocean — especially in the fast-changing Arctic — and named his wife, Diana Fox Carney, as Canada’s ocean envoy.

items: Oil and gas emissions rising as other sectors mostly flat, federal data shows

blocks.text: Sien Van den broeke, a campaigner with Greenpeace Canada, says the Halifax conference will be a place for countries to showcase commitments they’re making on oceans protection. She expects Canada will make some promises of its own, too.

With the new global treaty, Canada could also support new protection proposals off its vast coastlines. Van den broeke pointed to the Emperor Seamounts, a biodiversity hotspot in the northern Pacific, and the Sargasso Sea, another important ecosystem in the Atlantic, as potential areas the country could champion.

But advocates are also watching nervously as the Carney government has weakened environmental rules back at home, as part of the prime minister's agenda to build major new infrastructure and resource projects amid the ongoing trade conflict with the U.S.

items: In an unprecedented warning, leading climate think-tank says Canada won't meet 2030 climate target
Carney says Trudeau-era climate plan was 'too expensive' and 'divisive'

blocks.text: Canada has protected about 14 per cent of its lands and 15.5 per cent of its oceans, according to the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society (CPAWS). Its president, Sandra Schwartz, said that protecting nature is more than just hitting numerical targets.
“Nature really is quite foundational to our way of life and to our long-term success,” she said. “And that's both in terms of economic success as well as our overall well-being.”

As the host country of the 2022 conference that landed the global deal, Canada should lead by example, Schwartz said. But this month, the Carney government introduced a new law that will significantly speed up the federal environmental review process and change how oil and gas pipelines are assessed.
Carney faces climate, labour pushback over new nation-building bill
That comes on top of laws to designate and speed up major projects that have received widespread pushback from environmental groups.
“Canada's going to fall behind,” said Schwartz.
“And it's unfortunate that we appear to be pitting the environment against the economy.”

Coalition talks underway in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
Coalition talks are underway in the Baltic state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The Social Democrats (SPD) are meant to meet with the Green Party to talk about forming a government. The SPD met with the socialist Left Party yesterday too.
A coalition between the Social Democrats, the Greens, and the Left Party is the only viable option in the state to keep the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) out of the math.
The AfD won the contest in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania with 38.2% of the vote but has no option to govern the state since none of the other parties will work with it.
The SPD, which has long governed the state, finished second with 35.5% of the vote.

articles.title: Philippine Coast Guard drives off Chinese militia vessel, 24 boats near Kota Island
articles.summary: The PCG condemned the presence of Chinese militia vessels, saying it is China’s strategy to bolster its presence in the disputed territorial sea.

blocks.text: September 29, 2026 | 3:51pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said it drove away a Chinese maritime militia vessel and 24 smaller boats on Monday, September 28, after they were found allegedly fishing illegally in the territorial sea of Kota Island in the Kalayaan Island Group.

In a statement on Tuesday, September 29, PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Commodore Jay Tarriela said the Chinese militia vessel was monitored about 1.2 nautical miles northwest of Kota Island at around 10 a.m.
It then launched 24 small boats or “sampans” manned by two individuals, which spread out within 300 yards of the island at about 50-yard intervals.
Tarriela said the PCG deployed a five-man team from Coast Guard Station Kota on a rubber boat to challenge the vessels at around 11 a.m.
The crews of the vessel, however, only acknowledged the PCG’s instructions through hand signals and ignored the radio challenge.
The vessel and its small boats left the area upon the PCG’s arrival, according to Tarriela.
The PCG official condemned the presence of Chinese militia vessels, saying it is China’s strategy to bolster its presence in the disputed territorial sea.

“Launching two dozen small boats from a single militia platform is a force-multiplying tactic that extends the mothership's reach and reinforces Chinese presence under a civilian appearance, below the threshold of overt coercion,” Tarriela said.
Kota Island is among the land features within the Kalayaan Island Group of the Spratly Islands under Kalayaan town in Palawan.
The Kalayaan Island Group is a central part of the maritime and territorial disputes in the South China Sea, with China claiming sovereignty over nearly the entire area.
China’s claims were found lacking basis by a 2016 ruling of the international arbitral tribunal under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).
The ruling, however, was rejected by China.
“Fishing by foreign vessels within its territorial sea, without Philippine authority, violates Philippine sovereignty, Philippine fisheries laws, and the UNCLOS,” Tarriela said.
Authorities said they will continue to repel foreign vessels in the area as they continue to reinforce the PCG’s presence.

Key events

21m agoBurnham is told axing pension triple lock would be ‘electoral suicide’ as he prepares to address Labour conference

blocks.text: Burnham is told axing pension triple lock would be ‘electoral suicide’ as he prepares to address Labour conference

Good morning. The day after Donald Trump won his first US presidential election in 2016, Ed Miliband (at that point just an ex Labour leader) went on the World at One and gave an astute assessment of the lessons to be learnt from Trump by progressives. Trump was offering “big solutions”, he said – a theory he later fleshed out in a book called “Go Big”. Jeremy Corbyn was Labour leader at the time, and he certainly offered voters a “Go Big” vision – but for various reasons he could not persuade the electorate. But today a more mainstream Labour leader is also going to embrace “Go Big”.

According to the Labour party’s overnight briefing, Andy Burnham is going to use his first conference speech as leader to set out what he will describe as “a more serious prospectus for Britain than people have been offered in a generation”.
Burnham will say:
double quotation markWe can’t carry on as we are. Politics-as-usual has taken Britain backwards. More of the same isn’t good enough and isn’t going to get us where we need to be.

According to the Labour briefing, Burnham will say this will require “honest conversation” with the public and taking on the difficult issues that have been ignored for too long by Westminster, including social care, youth unemployment, and the need for greater public control of energy, water and housing. He will say:
double quotation markHope comes from honesty and from saying the things politicians usually avoid.

As Kiran Stacey, Jessica Elgot and Pippa Crerar report in the Guardian splash, Burnham will take his first major step towards putting Britain’s utility companies into public control when he announces a new government-backed body to invest in the electricity grid.

blocks.caption: Guardian splash Photograph: Guardian

blocks.text: But, for most of the media, it looks as if the story of the day will be another “Go Big” gamble by Burnham. On Sunday he revealed for the first time that he wants to fight the election on a colossal promise – a pledge to set up an NHS-style care service, with care free at the point of delivery. He did not say how this would be funded, but over the past 24 hours Downing Street has done nothing to quash speculation that part of the proposal will involve getting rid of the pension triple lock. This is one of the sacred cows of British politics, conventionally viewed as untouchable (even though in private many politicians from all parties agree with the view of almost all reputable economists, which is that in the long run its costs are unsustainable.)

blocks.caption: Times splash Photograph: The Times/Times
Telegraph splash Photograph: Daily Telegraph/Telegraph
i splash Photograph: The i
Express splash Photograph: Daily Express

blocks.text: Burnham does not seem likely to say he will definitely fight the next election on a proposal to get rid of the triple lock. (Labour promised in its manifesto to keep it for this parliament, and Burnham is sticking to that.) “Government sources have suggested Burnham would signal his willingness to review the policy, but stop short of a pledge to scrap it altogether,” we report today in our splash. So it looks as if Burnham will launch a pre-election debate, in the hope that he can persuade the public that axing an expensive and badly-targeted perk for pensioners is a price worth paying for transformative reform to adult social care. In his LBC phone-in yesterday, Burnham accepted there was a chance voters might just say no.
One of the voters saying no is Sharon Graham, general secretary of Unite, one of the most powerful unions in the Labour party. Asked about getting rid of the triple lock, she told the Times:

double quotation markI think it would be almost electoral suicide. Morally, I just don’t think it’s the right thing. We’re the lowest in the G7 in terms of how much we spend on pensions. I think that’s an embarrassment, quite frankly, because we’re one of the six richest economies in the world. I think it would be an absolute disaster, it would send completely the wrong message. I cannot understand why we keep going back to pensioners.
Here is the agenda for the day.
10am: The conference opens. The first speaker in a debate on power to communities is Chris Byrant, the Northern Ireland secretary. Claire Ward, the mayor of the East Midlands, is also speaking.

10am: Lucy Powell, the deputy leader, speaks at a “what can Labour learn from its members” fringe event. Other ministers speaking at fringe events this morning include Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, and Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister.
Around 11.40am: Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, addresses the conference.
2pm: Andy Burnham gives his speech to the conference.
5pm: Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, and Alan Milburn, the former cabinet minister who has chaired a review on Neets, speak at a Tony Blair Institute fringe event.

Given that it will be a big day in British politics, we will have comments open later for a few hours. I do look at comments when they are open, but I can’t read them all and if you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

blocks.text: Lucy Powell says Labour committed to triple lock for this parliament - but won't say if it could go after election

Lucy Powell, the deputy Labour leader, has been doing a media round this morning. In interviews, she stressed that Labour is committed to keeping the pensions triple lock for the duration of this parliament. But she did not deny reports that Andy Burnham might use his speech to suggest that it should go in the next parliament. (See 8.40am.)
She told Sky News:

double quotation markWe are committed to the triple lock. It’s in our manifesto. The triple lock has really delivered for pensioners, in this country, over the course of this parliament … I don’t know what Andy’s going to say about that today, but I know that what he’s talking about is this big conversation about solving these big problems, but being really honest with people that they come at a cost. You can’t just solve the social care crisis without having the big conversations about how you’re going to do this.

articles.title: Sandiganbayan rejects Revilla’s 2nd motion to inhibit presiding justice
articles.summary: In a resolution dated September 24, the anti-graft court found Revilla’s motion to be without merit, ruling that Associate Justice Karl Miranda must proceed with his judicial duty to sit and…

blocks.text: September 29, 2026 | 3:23pm
MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Third Division has denied the Second Motion for Inhibition filed by former Sen. Bong Revilla, which sought the voluntary recusal of the division's chairperson.

In a resolution dated September 24, the anti-graft court found Revilla’s motion to be without merit, ruling that Associate Justice Karl Miranda must proceed with his judicial duty to sit and hear the case.

In rejecting Revilla’s motion, the anti-graft court reiterated that there is no ground for mandatory inhibition under Section 11, Canon III of the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability, which does not include a judge's relationship with the counsel of a party's witness.

While judges may voluntarily inhibit themselves for just and valid reasons, the court found that Revilla failed to present the clear and convincing evidence of arbitrariness required to prove bias or partiality.

“There must be clear and convincing evidence of acts or conduct clearly indicative of arbitrariness. In this regard, the court found that Revilla failed to demonstrate any arbitrary act or conduct that would warrant the recusal of Justice Miranda from participating in this case,” the Sandiganbayan’s resolution read.
Revilla reiterated concerns regarding Miranda’s brother, Buenaventura Miranda, who serves as counsel for former Undersecretary Roberto Bernardo, a witness in his malversation case.

The former lawmaker argued that Miranda and the Chavez Miranda Aseoche Law Offices (CMA Law) assisted Bernardo during the preliminary investigation, during his appearances as a witness, and potentially with his application for admission to the Witness Protection Program (WPP).

Revilla also claimed that Miranda relied heavily on Bernardo's allegedly uncorroborated testimony when he issued a Concurring and Dissenting Opinion, or "Separate Opinion," voting to deny Revilla's bail application.

Furthermore, Revilla pointed to an incident in February 2026, shortly before arraignment, where Justice Miranda allegedly approached the accused in the courtroom and encouraged them to look into the benefits of the Good Conduct and Time Allowance Law. Revilla argued that these remarks gave the impression that the judge had already prejudged the case and assumed the accused would face lengthy prison sentences.

Addressing the relationship between the Miranda brothers, the court emphasized that Bernardo is merely a witness, not a party to the case, and was presented by the prosecution rather than by the lawyer Miranda.
Regarding the participation of CMA Law and the attendance of lawyer Carl Mucho at the hearings, the court noted that Miranda is not part of and has no interest in CMA Law, nor is he related to Mucho.

The court also agreed with the prosecution that the authority to retain Bernardo in the WPP rests with the Department of Justice and the Office of the Ombudsman, making Revilla's claims of bias on this front purely speculative.
The court also defended Miranda’s opinion on the bail application, noting that it was replete with citations of other witness testimonies and documentary evidence.

The anti-graft court emphasized that a dissent simply demonstrates a difference in judicial interpretation and that adverse rulings, without more, do not prove bias or partiality warranting inhibition.

With regard to the remarks on the GCTA Law, the anti-graft court ruled that these remarks were not born out of prejudice, but rather reflected Miranda’s long history as a staunch advocate for restorative justice, prison reform, and the rights of PDLs.

“The court then enumerated Justice Miranda's efforts to promote the rights and welfare of all PDLs, which included the following: (1) he has continuously coordinated with the Bureau of Corrections, Bureau of Jail Management and Penology, as well as private persons and groups regarding assistance to and the plight of PDLs; (2) he taught at the college inside the New Bilibid Prison in Muntinlupa City; (3) he assisted in setting up E-DALAW facilities in various jail and correctional facilities; (4) he helped organized national competitions, exhibitions, and an auction for artworks made by PDLs; and (6) spoke on restorative justice and prison reform on various platform, including in a podcast of the Supreme Court where he also discussed good conduct time allowance in relation to prison reform and restorative justice.”

The anti-graft court added that advising the accused to know their legal rights is consistent with the court's duty to ensure due regard for the rights of the accused and cannot be equated with declaring a conviction.

“The court emphasized that advising the accused to know their legal rights cannot reasonably be equated with declaring that he will be convicted. If anything, providing information concerning a possible statutory benefit is consistent with the court's duty to ensure due regard to the rights of the accused,” the anti-graft court said.
Revilla is being charged with malversation over the alleged anomalous P92.8-million flood control project in Pandi, Bulacan.

articles.title: From Jamui to Delhi, the burden of safety from sexual assault cannot fall on women
articles.summary:
As outrage grows over cases​ of sexual violence, activists are demanding a shift from controlling women to confronting men’s behaviour. Plus, Tony Klor’s ‘hella dope’ city vlogs

As an Indian…

blocks.text: As an Indian woman, I often feel myself oscillating between states of anxiety or anger. The anxiety is about doing the mental maths of how to stay safe – thinking about what I’m wearing, where I am going and how I’ll get there, and so on. The anger is at the sheer absurdity of this, and the stories of of sexual violence and harassment I read about every day. I am not the only one.

Last week, two particularly enraging incidents captured national attention. First, a video showing a group of men accused of harassing and molesting two teenagers at night in Bihar’s Jamui went viral. Then, a 17-year-old, out with a friend in Delhi, was allegedly gang-raped in a park by men posing as police. After, women in Bihar told Outlook how the incident in Jamui triggers greater controls and pressure on them. In Delhi, authorities curbed access to public parks and a premier women’s college, Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), briefly moved classes online.

I have noticed this pattern repeatedly: after incidents of sexual violence go viral on social media, the fallout further ensnares women. We are the ones who get told to avoid certain places, regulate our behaviour, dress modestly or be home earlier, thereby placing the burden of escaping this menace on us. Feminist activist Kavita Krishnan has described this phenomenon as “perhaps the most widespread form of gender-based violence in India”.

Instead of figuring out why sexual violence remains entrenched in our society, how patriarchal agency perpetuates such violence or what kind of social conditioning is needed for men, women are instead expected to take up less public space. (It is another matter that women might not be safe even inside their own homes.)

Regulating women is easy because “it does not require any institutional cost and, most of all, it sends the signal to concerned parents that the problem is being handled”, says Meena Kandasamy, a feminist author, whose latest novel, Fieldwork As a Sex Object, is about a woman’s life being upturned when a deepfake video using her face goes viral. “Their target audience is not the young women who feel unsafe but the rest of society.”

In my experience, this repression happens at three levels: first in the realm of family, then in broader society, and ultimately by the state. It begins at home, under the guise of protection, with arbitrary curfews or dress codes. It gets reinforced at a community level with institutions and social groups through moral policing, victim-blaming and the expectation that women should not put themselves in “unsafe” situations.

Then there is the response of the state. Restricting access to parks after sunset can surely reduce the number of people in those places, but it doesn’t address why women are unsafe there. Harassment and sexual violence are, unfortunately, not tied to timings or daylight. And further restricting women’s lives is not the solution to injustices foisted on them. All three, Kandasamy says, consider women as a “problem to be handled”.

“She’s not a citizen (for the state), a member (for the community), or an adult (for the family). She is treated like an inanimate but precious object – like a diamond that has to be locked up to prevent theft,” she said.
‘Moral policing’ of the wrong target

blocks.caption: Indian women commuters board a women-only train carriage. Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPA

blocks.text: Women, however, are pushing back against this approach. In recent days, students from Delhi University have come out on the streets demanding safer public spaces including more street lighting, usable public toilets, more housing and scholarships for female students. Vedayana, 20, a student at Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), says locking up parks is not the solution: “If you are not putting up safety measures to make it accessible to women, then it is as good as saying that the park is only for men.”

The scale of the issue is devastatingly clear. A recently published survey of more than 4,000 women in New Delhi and Bengaluru, found that 65% of women in New Delhi and 29% in Bengaluru experienced harassment in public spaces in the past year.

Another 2024 study from India and Pakistan found that women’s overall mobility remains abysmally low, and what freedom they do have is almost entirely tied to education, employment or unpaid care work. Substantive mobility for leisure or pleasure is practically nonexistent.

Despite how widespread and urgent the problem is, the political response can further shake public confidence. A female minister from Bihar, commenting on the molestation video said: “Moral policing can be done in a more decent and elegant fashion.” Another minister from the state drew fire for describing it as an “isolated” incident”.

Minimising crimes against women reflects a political culture in which accountability becomes optional. Students such as Vedayana want this to change. Political parties, she tells me, should pledge to not give tickets or positions to anyone accused of sexual harassment. “We don’t want the leaders sitting at the top to perpetrate and preach rape culture,” she adds.

Parliament is not immune to accusations, either: the BJP politician Brij Bhushan Singh, who formerly headed the Wrestling Federation of India, was recently accused of sexual harassment by six female wrestlers – he denies the allegations, and was acquitted by a magistrate, in a case that is undergoing appeal. According to an analysis of 2024 parliamentarians by the Association for Democratic Reforms, 15 winning candidates declared cases related to crimes against women.

For Vedayana, changing the mentality has to begin early with families and the way boys are raised. “If you are in a position of authority, use it to influence people by speaking out against patriarchy and groom your sons first.”

Sri Lanka settled for silver, while Pakistan claimed the bronze after beating Bangladesh.

Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.text: An inquiry committee probing the theft of donations from Ayodhya’s Ram Temple has uncovered 105 instances of cash being removed or concealed. The thefts were caught on CCTV cameras.
According to a preliminary report, some of the accused allegedly hid the money on themselves during the process of counting donations and then walked out.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: Tony Klor showing India, and the rest of the world, the beauty of Satara. Photograph: Instagram

blocks.text: Tony Klor’s city vlogs from Indian towns are “hella dope,” to use his own words. The 32-year-old American has visited about 200 cities around the country, taking his Instagram followers to places that rarely feature on a travel itinerary.

It’s a treat to watch him having the time of his life. He marched with Anganwadi workers in Nashik chanting “pay my didis”, ribbed with middle-aged uncles sweating it out in a park, whom he christened “Nizamaddies”. Wandering through the mining town of Ballari, which he describes as “highkey vibey”, he films its temple, church and mosque.

“A lot of people who watch my videos are Indians and they have no idea about these magnificent places in India,” the tech professional-turned-content creator says. “India is like the easiest place to make a friend in the world. People invite me to their weddings on the street that I met five minutes before that. Hospitality is so, so next-level.”

articles.title: Malaysia begins controversial repatriation of asylum seekers to Myanmar
articles.summary: Human rights groups say some 5,000 returnees could face violence, persecution and forced conscription.

blocks.text: The Malaysian government has started repatriating around 5,000 asylum seekers from Myanmar, under a controversial deal agreed with Myanmar's military ruler Min Aung Hlaing.
Three ships from the Myanmar navy are scheduled to leave Malaysia later today carrying the first 1,476 returnees.
Human rights groups have condemned the repatriation, saying the returnees face violence, persecution and forced conscription into the Myanmar army.
Malaysia has described the repatriation as voluntary, but has barred the UN refugee agency from seeing or screening the returnees, who have been kept in detention centres.

According to Malaysian prime minister Anwar Ibrahim, these returnees will include Rohingyas: a persecuted Muslim minority who have sought sanctuary in Malaysia in large numbers after being driven out of Myanmar, where they are not recognised as citizens.

Anwar, whose popularity has fallen sharply this year, says he is responding to growing public hostility towards the large Rohingya population in Malaysia and has no choice but to negotiate with the Myanmar government over their return.
But the move signals a striking shift in attitude.

Anwar, a former political prisoner, has previously presented himself as a defender of human rights and freedom, and called for more to be done to help the Rohingyas. Under him, Malaysia has refused to recognise Min Aung Hlaing's regime, and has been one of the strongest voices in South East Asia pushing for a negotiated end to Myanmar's civil war.
What has changed?
Two things. First, increased economic strain on lower-income Malaysians since the Covid pandemic, which has stirred resentment of the Rohingyas.

Second, the febrile state of Malaysian politics since 2018, when a historic election unseated the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), the ethnic Malay party which had monopolised power for more than 60 years, leading to a revolving door of unstable coalition governments.
For many years there was strong public sympathy among Malaysians for their fellow Muslims in Myanmar.

In August 2017, a brutal campaign by the Myanmar military drove three quarters of a million Rohingyas out of their homes in Rakhine State and into neighbouring Bangladesh. In the years since, dire conditions in Bangladeshi refugee camps have driven those with enough money to make the perilous sea journey to Malaysia in search of sanctuary and work.

While the Malaysian navy and coastguard have long tried to block Rohingya boats from landing in Malaysia, many gotten in via other routes, and for a long time were tolerated. More than 200,000 are now believed to live there, most eking out basic livings from manual labour.

Sentiment among Malaysians started to shift during the pandemic, which hit the country's economy hard. At a time of heightened public fear over the new coronavirus, accusations against Rohingya migrants spread on social media, with demands for their deportation.
In response, the then-government hardened its attitude, saying Malaysia could accept no more refugees and ordering raids on communities believed to be harbouring illegal immigrants.
Much the same has happened in 2026.

In May, an online complaint claimed that Rohingyas had failed to dispose of animal waste properly after the Muslim Eid al Adha festival, igniting a viral social media campaign falsely accusing Rohingya leaders of demanding land and citizenship in Malaysia.
Shortly thereafter, an online petition on Change.org calling for Rohingyas to be kicked out of Malaysia received more than 400,000 signatures, before being taken down.

Given Anwar's one-time reputation as a champion of liberal values, he might have been expected to push back against this wave of hate and disinformation. He has said the Rohingyas should be treated humanely.

"We can arrest them, but do not beat, intimidate or humiliate them," he said in a recent podcast interview - although this is exactly what human rights groups have accused Malaysian officials of doing in immigration detention centres.
Nonetheless, Anwar insists that the Rohingya must be expelled.
"They have clearly become a burden," he said in the same interview. "A security burden, an economic burden and a source of hostility among the people."

Some of his former supporters have accused him of betraying his principles. The former head of the Malaysian Anti Corruption Commission, Latheefa Koya, says his decision is "disgraceful, amoral, and shames the nation in the eyes of the international community".

Anwar, though, is under great political pressure. Once described as a perpetual prime minister-in-waiting, he finally got the top job in 2022, but only by forming an uneasy coalition with his one-time adversaries UMNO. Since then he has seen his own popularity plunge and his party lose seats in recent local elections. He must call a general election by early 2028.
"He is in a corner, at his weakest point", says Tricia Yeoh, Director of the Asian Institute for Policy and Engagement at the University of Nottingham Malaysia.

"He has been forced to make concessions to his UMNO partners... There have been several corruption scandals, and his own party is divided. And after four years of telling voters this is what is required to maintain his fragile coalition, they are no longer willing to go along with that narrative."

Instead, Yeoh says, ethnic Malays, who make up more than half of the electorate, are responding to the well-trodden UMNO narrative that they need special support and protection from the state - the kind of racial politics which she says feeds fear and resentment of outsiders.
"It's the same narrative you hear in the rest of the world, about immigrants taking jobs, that we should not be spending our public funds on facilities for them."
However, it is not clear how any Rohingyas can be repatriated to Myanmar, where they are not recognised as citizens.

Rohingyas are not permitted to travel inside Myanmar, and are only allowed to live in Rakhine State, which borders Bangladesh. But nearly all of Rakhine State is now under the control of the insurgent Arakan Army, and subject to sustained bombardment by the Myanmar air force. On Monday, the day before the repatriation, the Arakan Army said two bombs killed 49 people at a market in the town of Kyauktaw.

The only place Rohingyas could conceivably be returned to is the state capital Sittwe - but it is besieged and isolated, and even there Rohingyas are confined to wretched camps which are critically short of food and medicine. Rights groups also fear that any men in the group could be forcibly conscripted into the army to fight in the civil war.
Neither Malaysia nor Myanmar have explained how these formidable obstacles can be overcome, nor how their planned repatriation can be consistent with humanitarian principles.

"We all dream of being able to return home one day," said Nur Sadek, a Rohingya refugee rights advocate, "but we want to return because it is safe and because we choose to — not because we are forced to.
"For me, the most important thing is that Rohingya and other refugees affected by this decision are listened to and treated with dignity."

articles.title: Rights group accuses Vietnam of abducting Australian and Norwegian activists
articles.summary: Vietnam says the men entered the country illegally and accused them of planning terrorist activities.

blocks.text: A pro-democracy group has accused the Vietnamese government of abducting two of its members, an Australian and a Norwegian citizen, in Cambodia and taking them back across the border.
Vietnamese authorities confirmed that they had arrested Tran Hiep and Nguyen Duc Thuan, but say they had entered the country using forged documents and planned to carry out terrorist activities.
It said the men had admitted to being members of Viet Tan, which Vietnam sees as a terrorist organisation.
Viet Tan called their arrest a "blatant fabrication intended to conceal the fact that the Viet Tan members were abducted in Cambodia and forcibly taken to Vietnam".

The group, which has members in Vietnam and abroad, said the two men had been travelling in the southern border district of Kaoh Andaet in Cambodia when they went missing and had not been heard from since 18 September.
Tran's wife, Chloe Dang, told Australian media he had been meeting pro-democracy activists in Cambodia and had no intention of travelling to Vietnam.
He was meant to meet her in Bangkok to board a return flight to Australia but never turned up, she said.
"He always knew there was a risk doing human rights work, but we never thought that this would happen," she told the ABC.
According to a Vietnamese state media report published on Monday, Tran and Nguyen were detained with a third man at the border in Tay Ninh province on 18 September.

The trio "confessed to being members of the terrorist organisation 'Viet Tan,' [and] carrying forged documents to illegally enter Vietnam in order to carry out terrorist and sabotage activities," the report said.

They were charged on Monday with membership of a terrorist organisation while an investigation continued "to clarify the criminal acts of the suspects in order to handle them according to the law", it said.

"A state orchestrating the abduction of individuals abroad and forcibly taking them to its territory is a serious act of transnational repression," said Viet Tan. "It violates Cambodia's sovereignty and the fundamental principles of international law."
The Viet Tan statement did not mention the third man, who was named by authorities as Thai Cong Truong Son.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said consular support was being provided to Tran's family.
"That's what Australian governments do for our citizens. And we'll continue to engage directly with the family."

"Vietnam authorities' confirmation that they detained [these] activists... demonstrates yet again that Hanoi is arguably the most vicious and pernicious practitioner of transnational repression today in Southeast Asia," Phil Robertson, Director of Asia Human Rights and Labor Advocates said in a statement.
"This latest act is an unacceptable outrage."
The Vietnamese and Cambodian authorities have been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Palestinian embassy thanks Philippines for joining UN walkout on Netanyahu
articles.summary: The Palestinian embassy in Manila on Monday, September 28, thanked the Philippine government for joining last week's walkout on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the United Nations, an…

blocks.text: September 29, 2026 | 12:23pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Palestinian embassy in Manila on Monday, September 28, thanked the Philippine government for joining last week's walkout on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the United Nations, an action it says demonstrated Manila's "principled position."

The walkout placed the Philippines, which has kept close relations with Israel for decades, among the dozens of delegations that exited the General Assembly hall as Netanyahu took the podium on September 24.

The Department of Foreign Affairs confirmed Manila's participation to Philstar.com on Sunday, after independent tallies of the protest, many drawn from video clips of the proceedings, had listed the Philippines among the countries that stayed back in the hall.

In its statement, the Embassy of the State of Palestine said it "expresses its sincere appreciation" to the government and the DFA for the delegation's stance at the assembly's 81st session, "including its participation in the walkout."

The embassy also welcomed the Philippines' "expressed concern over the grave humanitarian situation in Gaza, the advancement of the E1 settlement plan, and the continuing rise of settler violence in the West Bank."

"This position reflects the Philippines' commitment to international law, peace, and the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people," the embassy said. It also cited Palestinians' right to self-determination and Manila's support for a two-state solution.

Manila said it joined the walkout as a call for peace directed at all sides. DFA Spokesperson Analyn Ratonel told Philstar.com that the delegation walked out "in global solidarity for peace in the Middle East" and to urge all parties to stop unilateral actions that erode the conditions for peace.

Ratonel cited Israel's push to advance the E1 plan, along with rising settler violence in the West Bank, as "detrimental to finding a just, lasting and comprehensive solution to the Middle East conflict."
When asked about the walkout on Monday at a briefing, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro repeated the DFA's explanation.
'Consistent and principled'
Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro expressed the same calls for peace in her own speech to the General Assembly on Saturday, September 26.

"We reiterate our call for an immediate and sustained ceasefire in Gaza," Lazaro said. She reaffirmed Manila's "consistent and principled support for the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people."
The Philippines–Palestine Friendship Association, a Manila-based group, also welcomed the walkout.
The group said solidarity with Palestinians had never been more important, citing what it called Israel's "continuing genocide, occupation, and war crimes."

"This is proof that governments can no longer afford to be passive spectators. The times demand that the international community stand on the side of humanity, justice, and the Palestinian people's right to self-determination," the group said in a statement.
This was the third straight year that Netanyahu's General Assembly address drew a walkout.
After briefly pausing at the sight of delegates streaming toward the exit, Netanyahu opened his speech by telling any "moral cowards" still in their seats to leave.

In a September 17 statement, the DFA had already flagged E1 and settler violence, warning that both "may contravene international law." That statement came about a month after Israel opened bids for over 1,000 housing units in E1.
Dozens of countries have warned that the project would split the West Bank and break up Palestinian territory.

Settler attacks, demolitions and evictions forced more Palestinians from their homes from January to April 2026 than in the whole of 2025, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.

articles.title: US ban on Canadian alcohol and dairy comes into effect as trade war drags on
articles.summary: It is the latest escalation in the Canada-US trade war after negotiations collapsed in late August, with no word on when talks may resume.

blocks.text: A US ban on several Canadian imports, including alcohol, dairy and motorcycles, has come into effect as a trade war between the two neighbours drags on.
The latest measure by the Trump administration is in response to Canada's implementation of tariffs on a range of US goods earlier this month following a breakdown in trade talks.
Canada is not expected to retaliate further, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying earlier this month that the impact the import bans will have on Canada's economy is "modest".
Trade talks remain on ice, with US trade representative Jamieson Greer telling CNBC recently that President Donald Trump is "comfortable" with his current relationship with Canada.

"They call us now and then and we have good conversations about potential deals. But there's no urgency on our side," Greer said of relations with Canada in an interview with the US network last week.
Tuesday's trade ban applies to nearly C$1bn ($710m; £530m) worth of Canadian liquor exported to the US, as well as whey products used in protein powder.

Motorcycle exports to the US will also be impacted, though Canada only sent about 5,000 motorcycles south of the border in 2025 that were worth about C$120m, according to national data by Statistics Canada, meaning the impact would be limited.

The import bans were first announced by Trump in a series of executive orders signed on 8 September. In them, Trump said the measures are in response to "continued discrimination" by Canada on US dairy, automotives and alcohol.
Speaking to reports on Monday, he accused Canada of "treating the United States very unfairly".
"They have been one of the worst countries in the entire world," Trump said.
Carney said earlier this month that the bans "are relatively modest measures" when compared to other trade actions the US has imposed on Canada.
He acknowledged, however, that the bans will hurt certain businesses and sectors that are directly targeted.
Derek Holt, an economist with Canadian bank Scotiabank, wrote in an analysis that "these actions are face-saving by the US administration, not substantive in nature and that's a positive".

About 93% of all Canadian liquor exports in 2025 were sold to the US. Spirits Canada, a group representing Canadian liquor producers, has said the consequences to the industry "could be significant"., external
Economists and businesses have also warned that the bans will add uncertainty to the future of Canada's trade relationship with the US, its largest trade partner.

In addition to these latest import bans, the US has imposed 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, including dairy, alcohol, steel and aluminium products, as well as 25% tariffs on Canadian-built cars.

Canada in return has placed retaliatory tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on more than 700 US products, as well as a 25% levy on certain steel and aluminium products. Most Canadian provinces have also stopped selling US liquor.
Tariffs - taxes paid on imported goods - are central to Trump's economic agenda, who argues that they raise government revenue and encourage consumers to buy American-made goods.
Economists, however, argue that they have raised prices of everyday goods for consumers and have disrupted the global economy.

articles.title: Argentina threatens legal action against UK over Falkland Islands oil exploration
articles.summary: President Javier Milei set a two-week deadline for the Sea Lion oilfield project to be scrapped.

blocks.text: Argentina's president has threatened to launch a legal challenge against the British government unless it halts oil exploration work off the coast of the Falkland Islands.
In a social media post, President Javier Milei set a two-week deadline for the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between Israeli and British companies, to be scrapped.
The companies insist they have valid licences issued by Britain.

The comments heighten tensions between the UK and Argentina over the sovereignty of the archipelago, known in Argentina as Las Malvinas, more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentine forces which had invaded the territory in 1982.

Milei said that if the two-week deadline was not met, he had "instructed the Foreign Ministry and legal teams to initiate international arbitration" against the UK over what he called "the illegal plundering of our resources through the Sea Lion Project".

He continued to warn the UK that if the "illegitimate exploitation" of the region didn't end within two weeks, Argentina would take the matter before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea.
The International Tribunal is an independent judicial body based in Hamburg which is responsible for the fair application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.
The move comes soon after Milei roundly criticised the UN in his speech at the General Assembly for failing to act over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands.
He said the UN had become "a useless organisation" which only serves "arrogant parasites dressed up as well-intentioned bureaucrats".
Since then, the UK Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, said that Argentina "lacks the ability" to take back the Falklands by force.

articles.title: OpenAI shelves new AI model amid safety concerns
articles.summary: The decision comes amid a broader push within the industry to slow the development of increasingly powerful and autonomous systems until safety measures can catch up.

image.caption: OpenAI and other AI companies are facing growing pressure to strengthen safeguards around increasingly autonomous modelsImage: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Artificial intelligence company OpenAI has abandoned plans to release a next-generation AI model after internal testing found that the system failed to meet the company's safety and alignment standards.

GPT-6.1 Astra, which is designed to handle increasingly complex tasks with less human intervention, had been scheduled to debut in October but tests reportedly found that the model displayed higher levels of deceptive behavior than its predecessors.

Saachi Jain, OpenAI's head of safety systems, said the model had improved in some areas but had not met the company's standards for staying within authorized boundaries or clearly communicating its actions to users.

"We want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's in the company, or when we ship it to users," Jain said. "But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms ⁠of safety and ​alignment."
Pressure builds for stronger AI oversight
The postponement comes as OpenAI and other AI companies face growing pressure to strengthen safeguards around increasingly powerful and autonomous models.
Some of these models developed by OpenAI and rival lab Anthropic have been involved in security incidents during testing.

Earlier this month, OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman and Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei joined other industry leaders in calling for a slower pace of AI development and stronger safety measures.
Leading AI executives are set to meet with US President Donald Trump in Washington on Tuesday to discuss the need for finding a balance between AI innovation and oversight.
OpenAI pledges to rebuild trust after government website hack
On Tuesday, OpenAI admitted that its models had even accessed Australian government websites and systems without authorization as part of internal training and evaluation exercises in June.

The company said ‌the activity ‌involved ​websites and systems linked to Services Australia, ​the NSW Bureau of ⁠Crime ​Statistics and Research, ​the Victorian ​Department of ‌Health and the Australian ​Institute ⁠of Health and ⁠Welfare.
The incursion, which occurred in June, was not made public until last week.
In a blog post, the ChatGPT maker apologized for the hacking and acknowledged it ‌mishandled its response ⁠and ⁠pledged to take accountability to "rebuild trust with the Australian people."

articles.title: France: Student protests over conditions at French high schools fuel political clashes
articles.summary: Over 160 people were arrested and dozens injured after student protests in France descended into violence. With a presidential election approaching, senior politicians are pointing fingers at each…

image.caption: The student protests began in the Ile-de-France region around the capital, Paris, but on Monday spread to other regionsImage: CLPRESS/abaca/picture alliance

blocks.text: Student protests spread to high schools across France on Monday, resulting in dozens of injuries, over 160 arrests and arguments between senior politicians — a day ahead of a nationwide strike by public sector workers and seven months ahead of the presidential election.

Teenagers at French lycées (equivalent to US high schools) have been blockading their schools since last week in protest at overcrowded classes, heavy workloads, poor quality learning materials and teacher shortages.
The movement began in the Ile-de-France region around the capital, Paris, but on Monday spread to other regions including Lille in the north, Marseille in the south and Sedan in the east.
Video footage on French media showed student protesters lighting flares and firing fireworks, even inside a school building, while police officers responded with tear gas.

blocks.caption: Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the 'escalation' of the situation 'irresponsible'Image: Adnan Farzat/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: French student protests: what have politicians said?
As of Monday night, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez reported incidents at around 180 establishments resulting in 164 arrests and injuries to 12 students, three teachers and 12 police officers.
He acknowledged that the "difficulties of high schools must be heard and addressed" but said: "This wasn't about making demands, it was really violence in its purest form."
He added that "a number of individuals … were masked, equipped with fireworks in tubes and projectiles [and] clearly wanted to confront the internal security forces."

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the "escalation" of the situation "irresponsible" and said: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers."
'Hands off our youth!' French politicians clash over protests

Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that the protests, which he described as a "classic high school student movement," were being exploited by violent elements — and took aim at the left-wing La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) party and its presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
"There is a political hijacking of the blockades by elected officials from France Unbowed," he said.
Earlier on Monday, Mélenchon had accused the government of implementing a "crackdown" with "obvious racist undertones."
"Hands off our youth!" he wrote on social media, while encouraging LFI activists and officials to support the protests wherever they could.

Prime Minister Lecornu called the accusation of racism "an insult" and accused Mélenchon of "racializing a debate about student security and adding to division where a responsible politician should be looking to restore calm."
In the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis, the LFI-run local council called the students' demands "legitimate" and published a statement reading:

"Let [the authorities] come and talk to [the students] and see for themselves whether the youth are being instrumentalized, or whether they are simply capable of thinking, organizing themselves and defending their own study conditions and their future."
France: The camps under Paris bridges
France: strikes — and an election — to come

The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, the French union that defends the interests of high school students, said it would urge a nationwide blockade of schools on Tuesday — coinciding with planned strike action by public sector workers.
French primary school teachers' unions said they expected some 40% of teachers to be off work on Tuesday.

With a key presidential election only seven months away and incumbent President Emmanuel Macron constitutionally barred from standing for a third term, French politicians from across the ideological spectrum are seeking issues that resonate with voters.
Mélenchon, a 75-year-old veteran anti-capitalist who finished third in the 2022 presidential election, is popular among younger, left-leaning voters.

His LFI party was one of the left-wing outfits which joined the Nouveau Front Populaire (New Popular Front or NFP) coalition in 2024 to oppose the far-right Rassemblement National (National Rally or RN) in legislative elections.
The coalition beat the RN but the elections produced a divided parliament which has been dogged by political deadlock and votes of no-confidence.

Prime Minister Lecornu is still trying to build enough support to pass a 2027 state budget, but his government is besieged by opponents who are unwilling to accept spending cuts while energy costs continue to rise.
Leo makes first official papal visit to France in 18 years
